Title: Remarks at the 2017 Institutional Investors Conference
text: Remarks by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel at the 2017 Institutional Investors Conference 03/12/2017 Baudot-Trajtenberg Nadine Foreign exchange market Presentation Deputy Governor Dr. Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg participated yesterday (3.12.2017) at the annual conference for institutional investors in Eilat and gave a lecture on "Managing foreign exchange reserves at the Bank of Israel." The Deputy Governor explained that the foreign exchange reserves managed at the Bank of Israel serve as a "safety cushion" for the economy in times of emergency, are expected to reduce the damage of a possible economic crisis, and reduce the probability that such a crisis will break out. In addition, they lower the State of Israel's risk premium and have a positive effect on its credit rating. The Deputy Governor described the manner in which the adequate level of the foreign exchange reserves is determined when, by law, the Monetary Committee, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, is entitled to change the principles on the basis of which the Governor determines the desired level of the long-term reserves. The principles are based on an integrated approach that takes into account international standards and an estimate of the possible uses of the reserves, with reference to Israel's special situation. The principles were formulated over the years, and the document of principles was approved in 2012. In 2015, the Governor updated the appropriate level to a range of 70-110 billion. In addition, the Bank of Israel has the authority to purchase or sell foreign currency, as one of the tools in the toolbox of monetary policy. Since 2010, there has been an increase in foreign exchange reserves from 60 billion to 111 billion at the end of October 2017. The ratio of the reserves to GDP remained stable, and increased only moderately in recent years. In an international comparison, it can be seen that in small and open economies that are comparable to Israel, there has been an increase in foreign exchange reserves in recent years, and in some of them there has even been a sharp increase in the reserves relative to GDP. Later in the lecture, the Deputy Governor discussed how to manage the foreign exchange reserves, with the three main objectives being: maintaining purchasing power, maintaining high liquidity, and achieving an adequate return that will cover the cost of financing. To this end, the Bank of Israel distributes investments among different countries and types of assets while maintaining the level of risk set by the Monetary Committee. The increase in the volume of foreign exchange reserves and the decline in yields worldwide led to their diversification on a variety of assets. In addition, the trend of diversification of the type of assets encompasses central banks around the world. Since the decision to purchase shares as part of the management of foreign exchange reserves, their contribution to the portfolio's yield has been positive. (Slide 22). In conclusion, the policy of managing the reserves at the Bank of Israel is not similar to the policy of another investment portfolio, due to the special characteristics of the foreign exchange reserves and the purpose for which they are intended to serve. The increase in the reserves portfolio made it possible to waive a certain degree of liquidity and increase the weight of risk assets in the portfolio. This process was carried out gradually and carefully, and earned the Bank of Israel the "Reserve Manager of the Year 2017" award by Central Banking magazine . As a result of the change in the composition of the portfolio, in recent years the yield on the reserves has been higher than the Bank of Israel's interest payments.

Title: Remarks at the Annual Conference for Directors
text: Remarks by the Supervisor of Banks at the Annual Conference for Directors 05/02/2019 Bar Hedva The role of the board of directors in the era of the fourth industrial revolution - the digital revolution Supervisor of Banks Dr. Hedva Ber opened the annual conference on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange this morning to update directors of the Association of Directors and the Association of Publicly Traded Companies. In her remarks, she referred to the role of theboard of directors in the current era, which is the era of the fourth industrial revolution - the digital revolution. From her words: The age of digital and automation has changed our lives and the lives of various companies in the economy. Companies from many industries are affected and will be affected by the digital-technological revolution: in retail, communications, tourism, industry, medicine, and in finance and banking. The great risk created for companies due to the digital revolution is that those who do not change  simply will not be. In a slightly less severe scenario, those who do not change will experience a significant negative impact on their profitability. Therefore, the question arises - what is required and expected of the board of directors in such a world? In my view, the board of directors mustlead the company's adaptation to the new world, technologically, business-wise and organizationally. I will reflect on a number of points on how the digital revolution is reflected in the world of banking:  the smartphone is becoming the main means of communication of customers with the bank, so that fewer and fewer people come to the branch; At the same time, customer satisfaction with digital services is very high (we saw this recently in a survey we conducted and published);  digital banks are being established around the world, which work without branches;  Automation enters many processes, both business and operational and replaces many employees in the service centers;  And most of all, technological and non-banking entities are entering the world of banking and becoming financial players that also provide various banking services. They are much more "thin" and efficient. In other words, competition in banking has increased greatly thanks to the digital revolution. Alongside the technological changes in banking, the revolution is also accompanied by complementary aspects unrelated to technology:  It is difficult for some customers to cope with the change, especially parts of the elderly population and those who are less technological. The public refers to the Banking Supervision Department complaints about the closure of branches of banks, the closure of tellers, and we demand that the banks provide a response to these customers in a variety of ways, including leading digital training for those customers; Alongside this, we at the Banking Supervision Department also receive inquiries that sometimes the vending machines break down. The complaints are examined under supervision, and, if necessary, treated.  Alongside this, the change is reflected in the redundancy of many employees in the organization, employees whose activities are being replaced by technology. In other words, the change derived from the technological-digital revolution is not only technological: it is holistic, and touches both the company's employees and the company's customers. Therefore, the board of directors has a central role in leading the adaptation of companies to the new world. The Banking Supervision Department has made many changes to its directives in recent years with regard to the digital revolutionchanges that we expect the Board of Directors to lead. In my assessment, the changes are relevant for implementation in almost all companies in the economy in which directors serve: We made a change to our directive in relation to the Board of Directors (Proper Conduct of Banking Business Directive 301), and demanded:  The Board of Directors shall have at least one director with expertise and proven experience in the fields of technology.  o In a world of change, you need the right mix of board members. The board should include directors who specialize in "old-world" issues, as well as those from the "new world". It is impossible to lead a revolution and adaptation of the organization without having the expertise within the board of directors.  We recently demandedthat the Board of Directors appoint a dedicated committee on information technology andtechnological innovation. We have defined that the committee will have to discuss at a minimum of: oInformation technology strategy and policy, including information security, management and use of databases, technological innovation to support business innovation oHow the banking corporation is preparing for the banking of the future and for dealing with the challenges of technological innovation in general and disruptive innovation in particular oTechnological risk management, including information and cyber security risks In addition, at my annual meeting as supervisor together with the Banking Supervision Department team and each of the boards of directors at the various banks, we called on the board of directors:  To conduct dedicated training for the board of directors, in the fields of technology and innovation, in order to learn and delve into the changes. training that will deal with issues related to both business opportunities and various risks, training in topics such as automation, artificial intelligence, open banking, cloud, digitization and digital transformation; alongside training in cyber and information security in the new world; Implementation of automated tools for detecting online anomalies and fraud and more. The need for dedicated training is required for the board of directors both to lead the organization's strategy and to have the ability to challenge management.  We demanded that the boards of directors reexamine the suitability of the Bank's core systems for the new world. Today it is clear to all that in order to respond quickly to changes, organizations needITsystems that are flexible. Systems that will enable the definition of a new product and its rapid implementation in the field.  We encouraged the Board of Directors to discuss the various scenarios that may take place in the banking world as a result of the technological changes, while addressing the changes that are already happening in the world today.  For example, in China, we see how technology has enabled entities that started as companies in the world of e-commerce or even in the world of gaming, to become new banks and compete with existing banks. The boards of directors of banks in Israel must study the changes and ask themselves how they are preparing for a situation in which those companies, or similar ones, will begin to operate here and compete with them.  Alongside these, and since the revolution is not only technological, we issueda directive that encouraged the banks to significantly increase efficiency, in order to adjust their production function; That is, to move from a people-oriented production function, to a technology-oriented production function. As a result, the banks have become very efficient in recent years. This is not a simple but necessary process, done in a manner that respects the banks' employees, and is intended to ensure the banks' right to exist in the future as well.  In addition to all these, we called on the Board of Directorsto lead and support the management when making the major changes required in the organization. The changes are not easy  for managers, employees and also for some customers. In conclusion, the Board of Directors and each of the directors of the various companies in the economy have a very important role at the present time, beyond the traditional role of government and supervision, and that is to ensure that the organization is prepared to adapt itself to the technological-digital revolution, and to lead the preparations.

Title: Remarks at the Leadership Conference of the Pensioners' Union
text: Remarks by the Supervisor of Banks at the Leadership Conference of the Pensioners' Union 08/11/2017 Bar Hedva Supervisor of Banks Dr. Hedva Ber spoke today at a seminar of the Israel Pensioners' Union, which was dedicated, inter alia, to the implementation of digital banking. Following are the main points of the Supervisor's remarks:  The world of banking in Israel is changing both on the part of the new consumer who wants to consume everything conveniently and remotely, and on the part of the technological revolution.  Direct banking makes it possible to improve the service provided to customers, save a lot of time, reduce costs and control the financial situation more easily.  The Banking Supervision Department and the banking system have developed many tools to help senior citizens adapt to changes in the banking world, and I invite senior citizens to use these tools.  The Banking Supervision Department is attentive and works to help veteran customers adapt to the change, using a variety of new tools, and is appealing to senior citizens to make an effort to adapt to the new world. In her remarks, the Supervisor noted that direct banking makes it possible to carry out operations remotely without going to the branch, save a lot of time, and control the financial situation more easily. The Supervisor noted a number of examples of services that have been added in the past two years that indicate the improvement and convenience of the service: depositing checks on mobile, developing payment applications, online joining savings plans, and more. During the lecture, the Supervisor of Banks presented the variety of tools developed by the Banking Supervision Department and by the banking system to help senior citizens adapt to the new world, and the requirements of the Banking Supervision Department, which in some cases constitute threshold conditions for closing branches, such as: the arrival of mobile branches in nursing homes, the placement of attendants for assistance in branches, investment in digital education of customers, prioritization of the elderly in a call center, Automatic joining a discounted fee track for senior citizens, adding services on the ATMs, easily locating lost accounts  "Money Mountain 2" and more. The Supervisor encouraged senior citizens to make an effort to adapt to the new world, inter alia by assisting flight attendants in the branches to learn about the use of the ATM, participating in individual or group training offered by the Bank for the use of direct means, using call centers where full service can be provided by a banker, and more. At the end of the seminar, there was a lively discussion, in which the participants raised the challenges they encounter and their ways of coping, along with the understanding that technological progress cannot be stopped. The Supervisor noted that she understands the natural fear of the change, and at the same time, the adjustment is feasible, and emphasized that senior citizens are not alone, and that the Banking Supervision Department will continue to accompany them in the adjustment process.

Title: Remarks at the economic conference "End of 2017" of the MBT Supervision Alliance
text: Remarks by the Director of the Research Department, Prof. Michel Strawczynski, at the economic conference "End of 2017" of the MBT Supervision Alliance 10/12/2017 Strawczynski Michel Welfare Policy and Labor Market  Global growth forecasts were recently revised upward. The acceleration of activity, which is characteristic of both advanced and emerging economies, supports the growth of Israeli exports.  The global crisis that occurred at the end of the previous decade had a negative impact on exports and activity in the construction industry in the advanced economies, while in Israel the construction industry continued to expand. Despite the gradual recovery, the processes of increasing employment in advanced economies have not yet been exhausted, while in Israel employment has gradually increased and the labor market is near full employment.  A comparison of labor market indicators in Israel relative to the OECD average shows that the unemployment rate in Israel is lower, the rate of involuntary part-time jobs is lower, the job vacancy rate relative to the number of unemployed is higher, and the rate of wage increases is higher.  The increase in wages has not yet translated into an increase in the inflation rate in Israel, which continues to be low as a result of the appreciation of the shekel, the intensification of competition and changes in consumer behavior, and one-off price reductions made in recent years.  Against the background of the state of the economy, there is currently no need for an active macroeconomic policy of the government through the budgetand in particular, it is advisable to avoid initiated tax reductions that are liable to increase the budget deficit in the coming years. In recent months, investment houses around the world have revised their growth forecasts for 2018 upward, and the improvement is expected in both advanced and emerging markets. Thus, for example, in the eurozone, which lagged behind in the exit from the crisis, the growth forecast was increased by 0.4 percentage points, and in 2018 growth of 1.8 percent is expected. These updates make it possible to assess that the increase in demand for Israeli exports will lead to continued growth in Israel as well, after the GDP growth rate in the third quarter was about 4 percent in annual terms. While the advanced economies were severely affected by the global crisis that occurred at the end of the previous decade due to the combined decline in exports and investment (particularly in the construction industry), Israel went through the crisis more smoothly, due to the resilience of the financial system and the continued growth in activity in the construction industry. As a result of continued growth, employment in Israel increased as it approached full employment. A comparison of labor market indicators shows that the employment situation in Israel is better than the OECD average. In most parameters: the unemployment rate is lower, the rate of involuntary part-time jobs is lower, the job vacancy rate as a percentage of the unemployed is higher, and the rate of wage increases is higher (attached charts). One would expect that the increase in wages and the approach to full employment would lead to an increase in the inflation rate, but this did not actually occur due to the appreciation of the shekel, increased competition in the economy, and price reductions initiated by the government in various areas such as auto, water, and telephone insurance. Against the background of the economy's approach to full employment, it can be assessed that no special measures are required in the budget in order to encourage economic activity, since it is on a path of continued expansion. Although the deficit is currently lower than the target set in the budget, initiated tax reductions will reduce tax rates on a permanent basis, thereby making it difficult to meet the deficit target in the coming years. In addition, the tax reduction in a situation of full employment is expected to have a relatively small impact on economic activity. Figure 1 Figure 2

Title: Remarks at the press briefing on monetary policy held today at the Bank of Israel
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Israel at the press briefing on monetary policy held today at the Bank of Israel 10/07/2017 Corneal Flug Monetary policy and inflation Research Department Staff Forecast, July 2017 Interest Rate Announcement, July 10, 2017 Watch the press briefing, Summary of the press briefing Hello everyone, As you know, the Monetary Committee decided today to keep the interest rate at 0.1 percent, and reiterated that it intends to keep the accommodative policy in place for as long as necessary in order to entrench the inflation environment within the target range. The Research Department published its updated macroeconomic forecast, which I will refer to later. Since we met here at the previous monetary briefing, the inflation environment has been slightly volatile, but remains below the target. The picture of economic activity remains strong. The rate of appreciation in the nominal effective exchange rate moderated with significant intervention by the Bank of Israel in the foreign exchange market, but the level of the exchange rate is appreciated. In the global economy, moderate recovery continues, but the ultra-accommodative monetary policy still continues in Europe, Japan, and other economies. I will now expand on these developments and the manner in which they are expected to have an impact on policy. In the past year, there has been a moderate increase in the inflation rate, and in recent months it has stabilized slightly below the target range. The higher inflation worldwide and the increase in wages in the economy contribute to an increase in inflation, but they are faced with the appreciation of the shekel, the halt in the increase in energy prices, government measures to reduce the cost of living, and changes in consumer behavior and competition in the economy, which moderate inflation. These are expected to lead to a decline in the annual inflation rate in the coming months, before it returns to increase toward the target range. Despite the increase in short-term expectations in recent months, they remain below the target, and are apparently affected to a large extent by the appreciation of the shekel, and by the fact that its effect on inflation may not have been exhausted to a large extent. Medium- and long-term expectations range throughout the period within the target range, so that market participants do not question the credibility of the inflation target regime, but believe that it will take time for the processes that I have described to be exhausted and annual inflation to return to within the target range. Economic activity continues to grow at a satisfactory rate. Net of the anomalous effect of the fluctuations in vehicle imports, the economy has been growing for the past year and a half at an annual rate of about 4 percent, and recent indicators allow us to assess that this growth will also be reflected in second quarter data. After a long period in which private consumption led growth, there are increasing signs that the economy is now returning to more balanced growth, with exports and investments also contributing to growth. The effect of the appreciated exchange rate is evident mainly in goods exports, while services exports are growing at a solid pace. Over time, against the background of the appreciation, the performance of goods exports was weak compared with the increase in world trade, while services exports increased at a faster rate than that derived from world trade in services. The unemployment rate is very lowboth historically and by international comparisonand the slight increase recorded in the most recent data is the result of an increase in the participation rate, rather than a shortage of jobs. On the contrary, many industries actually report a shortage of workers, as evidenced by the high level of the job vacancy rate. In the past six months, home prices have stabilized, and a variety of data from the housing market indicate that the market is cooling down: the decline in the number of transactions continues, and the monthly rate of new mortgages taken out moderated, even though the increase in mortgage interest rates halted. The government's efforts to continue increasing the supply of homes will support the stabilization of prices and subsequently their decline. In the global economy, the moderate improvement that we have seen in recent months continues. Forecasts have generally been revised upward recently, and the improvement in the growth rate of world trade continues. The positive momentum is notable in Europe against the background of political developments that reduced the risk to the continued existence of the eurozone and the European Union. Growth there is becoming entrenched with a continued decline in unemployment, although inflation remains below the target. In the US, there appears to be an improvement in growth after first quarter growth was disappointing, However, there is uncertainty regarding the administration's ability to implement the economic plans it announced. The Fe d increased, as expected, the interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, and its future rate of increase is expected to be moderate. The Fed He also revealed the details of the plan through which he would begin the process of reducing the balance sheet, but did not specify an exact date for its commencement. In Europe and Japan, the very accommodative monetary policy continues. The financial markets interpreted the ECB's messages as an indication that the strength of monetary accommodation is expected to contract, and this is reflected in an increase in yields on government bonds. However, the ECB Did not give an indication of when he would begin to withdraw from quantitative easing. After a sharp appreciation in the effective exchange rate in the first months of the year, the rate of appreciation moderated: in the past three months, in which the Bank of Israel purchased foreign exchange totaling about 3 billion, there was an effective nominal appreciation of 1 percent, with a relatively sharp change in cross exchange rates: the shekel strengthened by more than 3 percent against the dollar during this period, but weakened by about 3.5 percent against the euro. As we have said in the past, the level of the exchange rate partly reflects the relatively good state of the Israeli economy, which is reflected, for example, in a current account surplus and in relatively high growth. However, in our assessment, and in the assessment of other factors in the market, the exchange rate is overvalued, which is the result of the very accommodative policy adopted by some central banks. The level of the exchange rate makes it difficult for exports, with an emphasis on manufacturing, and on tradable industries in general. Over time, in order to support these industries, the government must take policy measures that will lead to increased productivity: improving the business environment, improving human capital, and increasing investment in infrastructure (which in itself, as we showed in the Bank of Israel Report, can contribute to a depreciation of the exchange rate). The continued monetary contraction in the US, and a change in the trend of monetary policy that is very accommodative in Europe and other economies, when it occurs, will in themselves be a force for the weakening of the shekel. However, the Monetary Committee will act in the foreign exchange market to the extent that monetary policy needs dictate it. The Research Department presented its macroeconomic staff forecast to the Monetary Committee (which, as we recall, is a conditional forecast based on assumptions regarding exogenous variables) and published it to the public. In view of the high growth in recent quarters, the forecast for 2017, in which growth of 3.4 percent is expected, was revised upward, similar to the growth of 3.3 percent expected in 2018. The forecast was revised upward regarding the growth rate of exports over the next two years, in view of the improvement in world trade. Inflation is expected to enter the target range in about a year, although, as noted, it is expected to decline further before it resumes its increase. The interest rate path in the forecast is the same as that presented in the previous forecast. In conclusion, the Bank of Israel's monetary policy is influenced by what is happening in the global economy, but it is directed only at achieving domestic goals. In our assessment, the accommodative policy played a part in the economy growing at a satisfactory rate and the unemployment level extremely low. However, for various reasons that I have outlined, inflation is still below the target, and even if additional central banks begin to reduce monetary accommodation, the Monetary Committee intends to keep the accommodative policy in place for as long as necessary in order to entrench the inflation environment within the target range. Have a nice summer!

Title: Remarks at the "Conference of Academics" in Tira on Promoting and Integrating Arab Society into the Israeli Economy

Title: Remarks at a cabinet meeting on updating the budget plan for 2020-2022
text: Remarks by Bank of Israel Research Department Director Prof. Michel Strawczynski at a cabinet meeting on updating the budget plan for 2020-2022 13/01/2019 Strawczynski Michel Fiscal policy Asrequired by law, the Government is today discussing updating the deficit forecast for 2019-2022. According to the Ministry of Finance's forecast, the expected deficit in 2019 increased to 3.6 percent of GDP due to a decline in the revenue forecast (totaling NIS 6.5 billion) and an increase in the expected level of expenditure (NIS 3.3 billion) relative to the aggregates included in the state budget. This forecast is not materially different from the Bank of Israel's current assessment, which is based on the macroeconomic staff forecast recently published by the Research Department. The Treasury has proposed curbing the use of the "reserve of adjustments for the need" maintaining fiscal stability", which reduces the expected deficit to 3.5 percent of GDP. However, this level also deviates from the deficit target for the 2019 budget of 2.9 percent of GDP, a deficit level at which the debt to GDP ratio is expected to increase, and at least not to decrease. In view of the expected deficit level, it is important that the incumbent government refrain from making decisions that will raise the deficit even more this year. In addition, and as described in the fiscal survey published by the Bank of Israel in August and in the three-year forecast (numerator) presented at the cabinet meeting, marked deviations from the budget targets for 2020 through 2022 are expected. This situation reinforces the need to avoid deficit-expanding measures until the formation of the new government, even with regard to the years after 2019. The Bank of Israel recommends that the new government that will be formed after the elections decide, as soon as it is established, to adopt the measures required to converge on the multiyear deficit path decided upon by the government in the past, a move that will ensure a moderate and prolonged decline in the debt to GDP ratio.

Title: Remarks at a conference of the Information and Statistics Department on the occasion of the publication of the Statistical Perspective Report for 2018
text: Remarks by the Governor at a conference of the Information and Statistics Department on the occasion of the publication of the Statistical Perspective Report for 2018 14/03/2019 Yaron Amir Good morning First, I would like to congratulate the Bank of Israel's Information and Statistics Department on this conference, and on the publication of the interesting review, "Statistical Perspective 2018." This is the first annual publication of this year by the Bank of Israel, which makes available to the public interested in the financial system the main data and aggregates that the Bank collects and manages on an ongoing basis, while shining a spotlight on the main developments that have occurred in these data. as well as for special statistical issues that the Bank of Israel deals with and deals with. We are in a very interesting and special period in human history. It can be thought of as the information revolution. Whereas in the past the scope of information was limited and it was relatively simple to analyze it, today the amounts of information accessible to everyone are enormous. The wealth of information presents opportunities for businesses to improve their competitive situation and to establish and establish new business models on the basis of the many data available to them. Those who are educated to meet the challenge required to derive the right information and derive insights from it that make it possible to make the right decisions benefit from it. And there is another important aspect of this revolution; Whereas in the past the reference to infrastructure was mainly to physical or technological infrastructure, today the information that floods us is in itself a necessary infrastructure for any organization, and as an essential infrastructure it must be invested in and developed while allocating all the necessary resources. This revolution, of course, does not skip over economic policy makers, including the central banks and the Bank of Israel within them. Big data and microdata have significant potential for improving macroeconomic forecasting and monitoring financial stability in the economy, and the Bank of Israel is developing its capabilities in these areas, as well as on specific issues in the field of economic advice to the government. Our challenge is, as mentioned, the ability to contain huge amounts of data and analyze them correctly, and in the background, of course, to maintain the privacy of those behind that data. The global financial crisis of 2008 made it difficult for the world's regulatory bodies to meet this challenge. This is because it was particularly difficult to extract from the information in a short time the necessary insights regarding the developments that took place in the financial markets. At the same time, financial tools became more complex, financial actors became more sophisticated, and the financial markets themselves became global, and their effects were sometimes hidden from view. In the context of the subject of data and information, the above developments have resulted in more information, more diffuse and more complex for analysis. As a result, the international financial institutions have promoted clear and detailed standards for collecting and managing the information required to understand, analyze, and track the complex relationships in the financial markets, both at the individual level and at the integrative and systemic level. Many central banks were given a significant role that gave them greater responsibility, together with their partners in managing economic policy, in the field of maintaining financial stability. The need to monitor and monitor systemic risks has led to the implementation of macroprudential policies aimed at identifying systemic risks in their nascent stages, and to promote actions that will deal with them and limit their impact on the financial stability of the economy. These developments have increased the central banks' need for consistent, integrative data bases to support this policy. To this end, there has been a trend in recent years of increasing the collection of individual data that will enable the completion of information on the flow of capital in the economy between the financial system and the real system, and between them and abroad. That is, how, with what intensity and when, a risk that develops in one place may affect in other places. These developments pose a special challenge to the Bank of Israel in the area of establishing and managing huge detailed databases, on the one hand, and on the other hand, the ability to research and analyze the information, derive insights from it, and make correct decisions in real time. We are not a deserted island in the financial ocean. The Israeli economy is integrated into the global economy and as such we constantly strive to meet the strict international standards. Therefore, the Bank is required to report extensively to institutions that dictate these standards, such as the OECD, the BIS. and the International Monetary Fund. Compliance with these standards ensures maximum quality of information and provides consistent and comparable data on a uniform basis that contribute greatly to economic policy management and economic research. I would again like to congratulate the Information and Statistics Department on this conference and on the publication of the Statistical Perspective Report, which contributes greatly to the professional discourse that the Bank is conducting with the main financial players and with the public. Thank you

Title: The main points of remarks at the Aharon Institute conference in Nazareth: "Removing barriers to the development of Arab society as a lever for the growth of the Israeli economy"
text: The main points of remarks by Prof. Michel Strawczynski, Director of the Research Department, at the Aharon Institute conference in Nazareth: "Removing barriers to the development of Arab society as a lever for the growth of the Israeli economy" 15/07/2018 Strawczynski Michel  The long-term key to the professional development of Arab citizens lies in the removal of barriers in the field of education, while providing the younger generation with tools to expand the choice of professions in a wider variety than is currently taking place, similar to the variety chosen by the non-Haredi Jewish population.  The Psychometric Entrance Test (PET) scores of students who took the Arabic test show that the average score of students in all fields of study is lower than that of students who took the Hebrew test. With the exception of two fields of study, medicine, and the arts, film, and communications, where the ratio of the average score of examinees in Arabic to that of examinees in Hebrew was higher than 90%, in the other fields of study, including economics, engineering, computer science, and many subjects in the social sciences, the ratio is even lower, which illustrates the great difficulty of Arab students in admission to the university and the depth of adjustments that must be made to encourage academic studies in Arab society. The choice of professions in Arab society today is influenced by traditional patterns, and it is important to act to change the situation, since it makes it difficult for Arab citizens to integrate into high-paying jobs.  In the short term, it is important for the government to deal with the removal of barriers that hinder the arab society's ability to integrate into the labor market, mainly in view of the fact that the existence of two wage earners in the household significantly reduces the chances of being below the poverty line. The tools that the government must cultivate:  Vocational training courses, with the referral of students through the voucher mechanism in accordance with the unique characteristics of the changing labor market in Arab society. It is important that the courses are based on the professions of the future, while avoiding the distribution of vouchers to professions for which the demand is expected to decrease. Emphasizing arab society's awareness of the "work grant" (negative income tax) program. In particular, highlighting the change made in the Net Family program, which provides a financial addition to families with two breadwinners.  Analysis of the factors that prevent the full realization of the "Employment Circles" program in Arab society.  Checking the suitability of the daycare system in the Arab sector, and making the necessary changes so that the system will provide a response to the departure for work of the two breadwinners.  A plan for the development of Arab society must be implemented by a joint headquarters of the government with the municipal and civil leadership in Arab society. It is important that the local leadership contributes its knowledge on the ground to remove existing barriers.  It is important that the local Arab leadership be involved in drawing up urban development plans; It is also desirable that it be involved in promoting infrastructure for technological studies and in establishing colleges  in order to ensure a future change in the selection of a variety of professions that guarantee high wages.

Title: Lecture at TheMarker's Economics and Society Conference in Be'er Sheva
text: The Governor of the Bank of Israel's lecture at TheMarker's Economics and Society Conference this morning in Be'er Sheva 22/11/2016 Corneal Flug The economy and economic activity Governor of the Bank of Israel:  We must take advantage of the good state of the economy to address the fundamental problems of the Israeli economy and society, in order to achieve growth that will reach all strata of the population.  Addressing some of the problems requires shifting and increasing budgets, but there arealso changes and reforms that can be carried out without significant budgetary cost.  Regulation and bureaucracy in Israel make it difficult to do business and sometimes the entry of new competitors. Israel ranks low by international comparison in terms of bureaucratic and regulatory burden, and our position in the indices is deteriorating.  Strategic activity on the part of the government and the promotion of structural reforms will contribute significantly to growth and are expected to bear fruit within 3 years (without the need for an additional budget!) Action should be taken to remove barriers to competition, such as standardization and regulation; reducing bureaucracy and improving communication between government ministries and between them and the citizen; improving and streamlining existing regulation, and more.  The sooner we adopt a strategic plan and implement it, the sooner we will be able to deal with the challenges and realize the potential inherent in the Israeli economy. The Israeli economy is in a good general macroeconomic situation, mainly given the relatively weak global economic environment: third quarter growth data published last week confirmed our assessment, according to which growth continues at a solid pace. The labor market is robust, and this is reflected, inter alia, in the rapid growth in employment and the continued decline in the unemployment rate to historically low levels, and in a prolonged increase in wages. Inflation has for some time been below the target range, but unless the decline in commodity and energy prices resumes, inflation is expected to return to within the target range within about a year, supported by the increase in wages. Against the background of the relatively good macroeconomic situation, it is worth focusing on addressing the economy's long-term challenges, which will help the economy to maintain inclusive and sustainable growth. The challenges facing the economy are in many and varied areas, and the Bank of Israel frequently analyzes and presents them, and I have spoken about many of them on various occasions. Addressing the challengesrequires reforms in a variety of areas. Some of the reforms involve a high budgetary cost (such asupgrading the human capital at all levels of education and vocational training, upgrading the physical infrastructure, and more), but there are also reforms that are very important to promote, and they do not involvea significant budgetary cost. In view of the fact that the budget for 2017/18 is currently in the process of being approved, I chose to focus today on the necessary reforms that do not involve a significant budgetary cost. I have presented the bleak picture of our poor position in the World Bank's Doing Business Index, which examines the business environment of various countries, and there has been no change for the better. In various areas that the index examines, such as the process of starting a business, obtaining building permits, processes in international trade, and asset registration, Israel is characterized by cumbersome and lengthy bureaucratic processes. Other Index, of the OECD, which examines the bureaucratic limitations on international trade, also indicates Israel's relative weakness. An updated OECD index of the rigidity of regulation in the product market, which consists of a series of sub-indices such as the complexity of regulatory processes or protection against competition by existing companies, also points to a bleak pictureIsrael ranks in the penultimate place, second only to Turkey. Indices of the rigidity of regulation in the retail and professional services industries also show that we are far from the international standard. Why is all this important? It turns out, if we quote the OECD economists, that "reforms in the product market, which mainly include a reduction in regulatory barriers to competition, can lead to a reduction in production costs, a reduction in export products, a decrease in raw material prices for industries at the bottom of the production chain, and an increase in productivity through increasing efficiency and increasing the quality of products by increasing the level of investments and innovation" (OECD"Going for Growth" 2016). ). In other words, reforms to improve the quality and efficiency of regulation can help the economy realize its growth potential even without increasing the quantity and quality of the production factors at its disposal, thereby contributing to growth in the short term. Moreover, such reforms can increase the incentive to invest, since they make the business environment friendlier and with greater certainty, thereby leading to an increase in the long-term growth potential. In the OECD's assessment, the significant contribution to the growth of such reforms can be felt within twoto three years after their implementation. According to an OECD examination, in Israel we are implementing reforms at a rate similar to the rate at which they are being implemented in other countries, meaning that in this area as well, the rate at which we are improving is not such that it is possible to closethe gap with the advanced economies. To try to illustrate the meaning of regulatory burden, I want to tell a story that was told to me and I asked for permission to tell you, while hiding the identifying details: The kibbutz in the south had a low tech factory. The factory operated in a 6,000-square-meter building built in the 1970s and 1980s. In recent years, the factory has not been able to compete with the import of its products from China and it was decided to close it, contributing to the fact that the building, which, as stated, was built many years ago, was issued a closure order due to the lack of fire extinguishing systems. At the end of 2013, the kibbutz decided to rent thebuilding to another industrial company. The tenant, Naturally, seeks to obtain a business license in order to operate legally in his new residence. What does the kibbutz need to do in order to obtain the long-awaited business license for the tenant? Here are the requirements: In the field of firefighting, it is required to set up a sprinkler system throughout the building, at a cost of NIS 700,000. The system requires feeding from a huge water tank, the size of 1,000 cubic meters, which is disconnected from Mekorot's pipes, and the cost of its construction is NIS 450,000 (an existing pool of the kibbutz, with a volume of 450 cubic meters, does not meet the requirements of the standard). Adjacent to the tank, it is required to place two pumps to create pressure. Why two? To be prepared for a situation in which, precisely when the fire breaks out, one of the pumps will be broken. Each pump should be backed up with an independent generator, in case just when the fire breaks out there is also a power outage. The two pumps together costNIS 500,000. That's not when we finished  the huge tank, which weighs 1,500 tons, needs to be placed on a concrete surface of the appropriate size and strength. Rather, such a pallet requires a building permit. As is well known, in order to obtain a building permit, you must obtain permits from the Israel Antiquities Authority, the Ministry of the Environment, and also from the Ministry of Health (since this is a water tank, and although it is not intended for drinking, a sanitary plan must be prepared for the tank). In order to complete the firefighting system, a fire detection and warning system is required (not the one that will operate the sprinklers, but another one, which will activate the announcement and alert the fire department), at a cost of NIS 120,000, fire extinguishing stations (NIS 150,000) with water feed separate from that of the sprinkler network (NIS 30,000) and smoke release openings (about NIS 100,000).         ,   ,     .         ,    ,   100  ,  ..... 2  . ,    ....  .          .    ,          ,      .     With the start of work lastsummer for the construction of the water tank surface, a stop-work order was issued due to the lack of a building permit, which the kibbutz has been trying to obtain since 2014, and is not succeeding because it is included in the permit for protected areas, for which they have not yet reached an agreement with the Home Front Command; The sprinklers have been installed, but are not connected to water, because there is no tank, because there is no surface, because it cannot be erected because the Ministry of Health requires a sanitary plan. There is a building, there is a factory, but the licenses are still far away... Over NIS 3 million for the license to operate an existing building. With an area of 6000 square meters. And the bottom line  the factory and the kibbutz employ a kind of designated "regulatory clerk" whose job it is to obtain all these permits through architects, engineers, consultants and especially  "farmers" who promote the treatment and the queue and achieve relief without which there is no chance of reaching the long-awaited approval. The end of the story (for this time). Each of the regulators does its job faithfully; Each regulator sees only its own angle (and probably does not tend to take risks in its area of responsibility), and no one sees or internalizes the price paid by entrepreneurs and the economy for the delay in the construction of the enterprise, assuming that at the end of the road the long-awaited license will indeed be obtained before anyone gives up. Let us return to the discussion at the level of the entire economy. So what needs to be done? (Slide 19) In order to deal with the challenges, a focused strategic plan is required that will include: uContinued implementation of reforms to improve government regulation, for example througha one-stop-shop, which will have relevant powers and resources in regulation for business licensing, while adapting it to best practice in the OECD. uContinued efforts to reform and remove barriers that impede exposure to competition from around the world; Such as the unification of standardization with the developed world and the easing of regulation in import processes. uInvestment and reforms in "network" industries such as public transport, railways, energy, ports, communications, and mail. uOnline transfer of information between government ministries, in particular regarding statutory approvals. The long term is here! The sooner we adopt a strategic plan focused on these issues, In this way, we will be able to deal with the challenges and maximize the potential of the economy.

Title: Remarks at the opening of the JEDG Forum for 2019 in Washington, D.C., USA
text: The words of the Governor of the Bank of Israel, Prof. Amir Yaron at the opening of the 2019 JEDG Forum in Washington, USA 10/25/2019 Yaron Amir macroeconomic policy The Governor of the Bank of Israel, Prof. Amir Yaron, participated in the joint forum for economic development between Israel and the USA (the (JEDG) for 2019 in Washington, USA. Governor Yaron delivered opening remarks at the conference, and then, as part of the first professional session, which dealt with a macroeconomic review of the Israeli economy, the Governor reviewed the key monetary and macroeconomic developments in the Israeli economy and in the world recently, touching on the tangents to Israel and the United States in various economic issues, and lists some of the moves completed at the Bank of Israel in the first year of his tenure. Attached are the governor's opening remarks (in English). JEDG (Joint Economic Development Group) - the Israel-United States Economic Development Forum, led by the Israeli Ministry of Finance and the American Departments of State and Treasury, and in cooperation with the American Chamber of Commerce. The JEDG forum, convenes once a year, and within it discusses the economic developments in Israel and the world and the creation of cooperation between the two countries. The conference serves as the main platform for the economic dialogue between Israel and the United States and is attended by key economic and diplomatic figures. The process of organizing the conference includes determining content, sections, and relevant participants, alongside producing progress reports on the topics covered in the previous conferences. I am very happy to have the opportunity to participate in these meetings, for the first time as Governor of the Bank of Israel. I saw the interesting and very full schedule, and I am sure that today will be productive for all the participants from both sides. The recent meetings in the IMF clearly point to more downside risks, and the various projections for growth and trade for most regions have been updated downward. Furthermore, many participants noted that the global uncertainty will make it more difficult to return to better growth prospects. Consequently, the economic discussions, as reflected in these meetings suggest that accommodative monetary policy is likely to stay for longer, yet responsible and growth enhancing fiscal policy is needed to support growthan area in which there is much room for potential collaborations. The discussions also dealt with the fundamental technological advancements affecting the banking and financial systems --- a feature providing many opportunities yet with potential new risks. To continue to function in a changing economic environment, and to know how best to move forward in the face of potential crises, we have to speak, think, and breathe innovationtechnological, financial, and research-related. To do this best, we have to initiate collaborations, precisely of the type through which we are here today, that assist in creating, exchanging ideas, and promoting joint initiativesutilizing the comparative advantages of each one of the participants. I will shortly review the main recent monetary and macroeconomic developments in the Israeli economy, and I will attempt to touch on the lines that reach both Israel and the US in some of the issues. However, at this time Id like to note, in short, several of the processes that we completed at the Bank of Israel in the first months of my tenuresome of which started in the years before my tenure started. In the financial area, we are progressing on a reform to promote competition, in full collaboration with the Minister of Finance: We brought online the Credit Data System, which is functioning satisfactorily. A large number of financial entities, including some that are not required to do so by law, have joined the system and begun reporting to it and receiving data from it. We also started off with the separation of two credit card companies from banks, while taking care that the parameters of the separation support the goals of the reform to promote competition in the financial system in Israel. And beyond all thiswe granted a license to a new, digital, bank, and we are assisting it so that it can begin operating soon. I am also happy to report that the Financial Stability Committee, which I head, has met several times already and is moving forward with formulating tools and work procedures. In the fiscal area, we presented the government with a comprehensive and clear analysis regarding the need to carry out fiscal adjustments. In parallel, we presented a plan to improve the standard of living and the productivity in the economyemphasizing operative policy proposals. In the research area, in a joint initiative with the IMF, we are developing a new macroeconomic model, which takes into account two areas that previously had not been included in the generally accepted modelsthe housing market and the financial system. Recall that these were among the main factors in the 2008 crisis. We will use the model for macro assessments, but it will also contribute to the work of the Financial Stability Committee. Thank you.
