Title: Remarks at the Inequality and Government Intervention Conference of the Bank of Israel Research Department
text: Remarks by the Governor at the Inequality and Government Intervention Conference of the Bank of Israel Research Department 26/06/2019 Yaron Amir Good morning Holding this conference at this time is of paramount importance, since its time, which has long been set, could not have been more successful in discussing issues of government intervention and inequality in Israeli society. It is very important that economic research in all matters related to these issues be professional and of high quality, using the most advanced research methods, so that policymakers have the best knowledge required to make informed decisions. In my remarks today, I will naturally deal with the issue of inequality in the Israeli economy. Inequality in Israel has a variety of aspects: the economic aspect, i.e., earning capacity, the skills aspect as expressed in academic achievements and labor market skills, and the opportunity aspect. First, let's look at inequality in Israel compared to other countries, as reflected in the Gini index of disposable income in OECD countries. It can be seen that inequality in Israel is high, but is not exceptional. At the same time, it should be noted that the incidence of poverty is high. It should be noted that the poverty line increases with economic growth, even when looking at it relative to GDP per capita. Nevertheless, the incidence of poverty in recent years has been on a downward trend. Anyway, Although the issue of poverty is important and tangential to the issue of inequality, later in the lecture I will focus on the issue of inequality and its various aspects. When looking at the development over time of the inequality index in Israel, we can see that for the past decade there has been a process of decline in disposable income inequality, after an increase in inequality in the previous decade. The decline in disposable income inequality is led by a reduction in inequality in economic income in Israel. The average number of earners per household has increased, but the most notable of all is the increase among the lowest income quintile. The increase in participation rates in all groups (and sectors) of the populationa combination of policies that encourage employment, together with cultural processes, alongside an increase in the minimum wage, and a continued decline in the unemployment levelsupport the process of reducing inequality in economic income and reducing disposable income inequality. Skills Skills are fundamental skills required in the modern labor market, as defined and examined by the OECDin an international survey of adults (PIAAC survey). The survey includes quantitative, verbal and problem solving tests in a computerized environment. We can see that a major factor influencing individuals' wages is their work skills, that is, exactly these skills. There is a strong statistical relationship between the scores on the skills test administered by the OECDand the wages of examinees. The average level of achievements on skills tests in Israel is low. Both on average the entire population, and when the analysis is reduced to include two population groups that are generally identified as having lower qualifications in the areas examined: the ultra-Orthodox public and the Arab sector. This is an important point, because sometimes it seems that assisting and promoting these populations will solve the problem of skills in the Israeli economy. This is not the case  this is a problem that concerns all population groups and requires comprehensive measures and policies, even if with specific reference to these groups. It is not surprising, then, that the return on the skills required in wages in Israel is among the highest among the comparison countries, since it is a resource in short supply. The variance in skills test scores in Israel is the highest among the countries included in the survey, both on average, excluding Arab society, and excluding both the ultra-Orthodox and the Arabs. In other words, the gaps in skills in Israel are striking in international comparison. As noted, these gaps place policymakers in their efforts to reduce inequality at a difficult starting point. We emphasize that the gaps in skills do not reflect a particularly high ability of the stronger population, but rather a weakness of the population with lower skills. This can be seen when comparing the results of the tests in Israel with the average in OECD countries, by deciles. The low level of skills of adults in Israel contrasts with a high level of formal education: both in the number of years of schooling and in the rates of higher education, which are third only to Japan and Canada worldwide. The level of skills in Israel is low at all levels of education compared to other countries, although the gaps narrow as the level of education increases. So, we have a kind of riddle here  how does it happen that the scope of those studying for higher education is extensive but the skills in the labor market are low? It is possible that the reason lies in the fact that the gaps in skills vis-a-vis abroad open at a relatively early stage, already in basic education. The performance of middle school students in Israel is very low compared to other advanced economies. Equal Opportunities It is possible that the high inequality in abilities among adults in Israel reflects gaps in talent, and these gaps can be addressed through social policies of supporting a weaker population. One way or another, it is very important to allow equal opportunities. Beyond the implications of social justice, equal opportunities can contribute to growth, as it improves efficiency. Equal opportunities at an early age may also reduce the gaps in skills that we see among older adults. It is therefore interesting to ask to what extent is equality of opportunity in Israel similar to that in other countries? The various findings dealing with this question are inconclusive. One indicator for examining the level of inequality in opportunities is the share of students from weak socioeconomic backgrounds who manage to reach the top quartile in achievements on the PISA exams. In Israel, the share of young adults (aged 15) among the population at a low socioeconomic level who succeed on the PISAexams is significantly lower than the OECD average. . This may be evidence that young people from the weaker population did not get an equal opportunity. The gap in PISAscores between the 95th and 5th percentiles in Israel is also the highest. Alongside these findings, it is worth noting that the gap in the average score on the PISAscience test between the upper socioeconomic quarter and the bottom quartile is not significantly higher than the OECD average. Another statistic that we can look at in order to examine equality of opportunity in Israel is the degree of intergenerational mobility. The intergenerational mobility figure is perhaps the best expression of equal opportunities, but data limitations and the long time that passes until the results are obtainedwe have to wait an entire generation for an answer as to whether intergenerational mobility has been identifiedgreatly undermine the relevance of this figure to current policy. An international comparison of intergenerational mobility is also not simple, mainly due to data limitations, since we need salary data for both the parents' and children's generations. Non-qualitative wage data (e.g., wage data that do not reflect permanent wages) may indicate a higher mobility than the one that actually occurs; An examination of the wages of the next generation when they are still young (and their wages do not yet reflect the permanent wages) may also indicate a higher mobility than actually exists. Therefore, the comparative data of intergenerational mobility obtained in various studies should be treated with the necessary caution. A look at the comparison of Israel with other countries, with all the caution required in analyzing these data, indicates intergenerational mobility in Israel that is similar to other countries, and when taking into account the starting point of the inequality in abilities that exists in the population, we can say that the situation in Israel even looks good. Another indicator is the likelihood that an individual whose parents are from the bottom quintile of the income distribution will belong to the top quintile in adulthood. As mentioned, making these comparisons is complicated and therefore here we see a total of 5 countries, and the figures in Israel are no different from those of the other four countries. Finally Inequality in Israel is high, but it is not unusual; A significant part of the inequality reflects differences in work skills, which constitutes a long-term challenge for policy, which should be addressed both from an overall perspective and while providing a response to relevant groups in the population, with their unique characteristics. However, despite the high inequality, the evidence to date points to intergenerational mobility that is similar to that which exists in other developed countries, which is certainly an encouraging sign. There is some evidence of weakness in equal opportunities in Israel, and it is important that attention be paid to this. Both for the proper social reasons and for the contribution to the economic growth of an economy in which equal opportunities exist. I would like to thank Prof. Giovanni Violante for coming to be the guest of honor at the conference. Prof. Violante is one of the world leaders in the field of creating databases that help understand the development of income, consumption and the labor market. These works contribute to the deepening of knowledge and the ability to carry out informed analysis on many issues, including the issue of inequality. They thought about deepening and advancing research on these issues at the Bank of Israel and in Israel in general.

Title: Remarks at the conference on Increased Management and Enforcement of Compliance Risks
text: Remarks by the Supervisor of Banks at the Israel Money Laundering Prohibition Authority's conference: Increased management and enforcement of compliance risks over the past decade: What has changed, what are the implications for customers, and what is required from here? 26/12/2017 Bar Hedva Dear Sirs, The Minister of Justice, the Attorney General, the Head of the Israel Money Laundering Prohibition Authority, the honorable ones, I am happy to take part in this important conference in honor of the 15th anniversary of the establishment of the Israel Money Laundering Prohibition Authority. Since the establishment of the Authority, there has been a major and very important change in the field of anti-money laundering in Israel, which has a major impact on the economy and society. In my remarks, I would like to give the Banking Supervision Department's perspective on the anti-money laundering regime in Israel, and in particular on the tightening of compliance risk management, when I will describe what has changed in these years, what the consequences are for customers, and what we think needs to be done from here. As is well known, the banking system in Israel offers a very wide range of products and services, designed to enable high-quality and advanced banking services for business and private customers, the vast majority of whom are law-abiding. However, in recent years, a significant tightening of the management of compliance risks at banks has been required and carried out, against the background of very significant legislative changes in Israel and abroad, and against the background of investigations of banks around the world by US authorities on compliance issues. Some of the investigations of Israeli banks into tax evasion by American customers have not yet been completed, and some have found failures. However, it is important to say that the American investigations are about past events, which reflected the "world of the past." Since then, lessons have been learned and the Banking Supervision Department's requirements have been significantly tightened, and the banks' compliance risks have been significantly tightened. These are the questions I would like to discuss today: First, have we not shifted the pendulum from one extreme to the other with regard to the demands of the banks and customers in the field of compliance? From the one end we were about 20 years ago - of lack of awareness and lack of handling of the issue, of a world in which individuals and companies managed deposits in the banks and the banks were not required to check whether the source of the funds was from illegal activity; To the other end that we are at today, where the expectation of the regulatory and enforcement bodies is that the banks will be their long arm in the field of money laundering, terrorist financing and tax evasion, Including enforcement of tax laws of foreign countries. All this, taking into account the fact that there are still nonbank entities in Israel that do not have a money laundering prohibition regime, which do not have a valid order, nor effective regulation and enforcement, but are interested in opening accounts in the banking system, which they perceive as an essential infrastructure for their activities. The second question is, what is the price paid by customers due to the very tight handling and strict enforcement of the banks in the field of compliance, customers who are innovative companies, new immigrants, charitable societies that work for the benefit of the public, non-residents, and more? I won't leave you in suspense: the answer is that the price is very high. And the third question is whether we should return the pendulum to a more balanced place, and if so, what should we do for that? I will begin with a brief description of the development of things, from the banking angle: In 2000, with the enactment of the Anti-Money Laundering Law in Israel, the change was reflected in the fact that banks were increasingly required to serve as a long arm of the various authorities in order to identify and prevent transfers of funds that are allegedly used for illegal activities, and particularly after the establishment of the Authority in 2002, they were even required to report on this. In other words, the banks and other financial institutions joined the war against serious crime and later also terrorism. The banks established large compliance systems, invested enormous resources, among other things, in computer systems and manpower, and changed all work processes with customers. Over the years, the Banking Supervision Department has implemented and enforced the change, the banks have tightened their approach in checking funds and customers and alerted the authorities when there were suspicious signs, and the authorities have even managed to stop, through the banks' warnings, many illegal activities. This is what the authorities have reported and are reporting to us to this day. At the end of the previous decade, the US began to lead a stricter line of larger-scale investigations against banks around the world regarding compliance aspects, while expanding the areas of enforcement to tax issues as well. In fact, the US changed the "rules of the game" in its dealings with countries, especially Switzerland, which was known for its bank secrecy, and as a result, banks around the world were fined hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars, For non-compliance with various laws. In this context, an investigation of three Israeli banks operating in Switzerland also began, in which it turned out that American customers of the banks did not pay tax to the American authorities, and that products that banks offered to customers that were also accepted around the world, made it easier for customers to evade tax. I would mention that at the time, Israeli law did not define the tax offense as a source offense in the Prohibition of Money Laundering Law. A change in the law in this aspect was carried out only in 2016. The Banking Supervision Department has learned lessons over the years from the US investigations, and sent an unequivocal message to Israeli banks that the Banking Supervision Department has no tolerance for compliance risks, including in cross-border operations. That is, if there is any doubt in aspects of compliance - there is no doubt: do not open the account and do not allow the transfer of funds. The reason is the great responsibility, on the personal and criminal levels, that may be imposed on a banker if and when a risk is realized in a customer's account. As a result, the banks have greatly tightened the controls on the accounts of all customers, and this is reflected in the fact that they are asking for more and more references from customers, A lot of questions are asked, funds are stopped that are not fully clear what their origin is, and the friction with customers increases greatly. The result is that we are currently receiving repeated complaints from many parties regarding the difficulty that these aggravations create for customers. In particular, we receive complaints about the banks' strict policies regarding non-residents, new immigrants, fintech companies, inter-person lending companies (PTPs), payment institutions, entities and individuals that deal with virtual currencies, as well as GMOs, currency service providers (NGOs), charitable institutions, and lawyers who manage trustsall of which are entities in which it is more difficult to identify the source of the money. Most of them are legitimate entities, However, their activities are complex and partly unregulated. There are those who claim that the reason that banks refuse to open accounts for these customers is that they are afraid of competition, but the analysis we conducted at the Banking Supervision Department regarding these cases shows that this is not the case. Banks manage accounts and extend large-scale credit to companies that directly compete with them. The reason for the difficulties experienced by some companies in opening and managing bank accounts is, as I mentioned, the risks of compliance. Against the background of the situation that we have reached, in which regulation and enforcement in the field of compliance risks lead to the fear of bankers and to damage to certain sectors of the economy, I call on regulators and enforcement agencies to sit together and think about what can be done to balance the pendulum a little. The following are some directions that we at the Bank of Israel believe should be advanced:  First, it is necessary to complete the regulation of the activities of fintech companies, PTP, GMOs, NGOs, and charitable institutions, to establish an anti-money laundering order, and to supervise these entities, so that they have the responsibility to serve as the "first line of defense" in managing compliance risks when they open a bank account. This is in order to enable them to operate more easily and to reduce friction with the banks. Today there are still many entities that operate in the economy without proper regulation and supervision.  In addition, it is important to publish an enforcement policy by the State Attorney, which will determine that when a compliance risk is realized, and there are risks that will be realized, there will be consideration of the general level of compliance at the Bank, similar to the outline defined by the Israel Securities Authority in the field of administrative enforcement, and that consultation with the regulator on this matter will be held. This policy should emphasize that an action in accordance with the directives of the regulator will be defined as an action taken by the bank in good faith. Thesupervisory bodies in Israel and around the world speak of the proportionality required in managing compliance risks. We certainly share this call, butit is important that the proportionality is also enforced, when the risk is realized, according to the outline as aforesaid.  In addition, in order to encourage innovation and competition in the financial field, it is advisable to define a "regulatory sandbox" (sand-box), which will allow fintech companies to enter it and easily open a bank account, while easing the compliance requirements of the banks with respect to these companies. We at the Bank of Israel believe that joint action is required by regulators and enforcement agencies, and that if we take these steps, we will succeed in reducing the fear created at the banks in the area of compliance and balancing the pendulum in favor of the activity of companies and individuals, most of whom have a positive contribution to the economy.

Title: Remarks at the press briefing on monetary policy held today at the Bank of Israel
text: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Israel at the press briefing on monetary policy held today at the Bank of Israel 06/04/2017 Corneal Flug Monetary policy and inflation Notify the interest rate To the macroeconomic forecast To view the Governor's remarks at the press conference Hello Everyone As you know, the Monetary Committee decided today Continue the accommodative monetary policy and keep the interest rate at 0.1 percent, noting that it intends to leave the accommodative policy in place, for as long as necessary to establish the environment Inflation within the target range. The Research Department published its updated macroeconomic staff forecast, And I will refer to it later. Since we met here at the previous monetary briefing, there have been Mixed developments in the inflation environmentactual inflation continues to increase moderately, but There has been a decline in expectations. The picture of strong economic activity that we saw at the end of 2016 is no different Essential even today, and I will expand on it later. In the foreign exchange market, the appreciation strengthened, which also affects The inflation environment as well as on activity, and therefore it was accompanied by a relatively sharp policy response through Foreign exchange purchases. Assessments of the global economy are slightly more optimistic now than they were before Three months, but political developments in various countries continue to be a factor Significant for uncertainty. I will expand, therefore, on how the Committee views the picture The situation now, and regarding the policy and its expected effects. In the past year, there has been a moderate increase in the pace Inflation, and after almost two years in which inflation was negative, at the beginning of 2017 inflation reversed positive, but it is still below the target range; This is despite the influence of factors of a one-time nature that acted Lowering inflation has dissipated, and in fact, for the past few months the increase in energy prices has been contributing A positive contribution to annual inflation. In the Bank of Israel Annual Report published last week, we showed that changes In consumer behavior, such as increasing online purchases, work to increase competition and therefore We continue to press for low inflation. This is a restructuring of price adjustment, which may take time What but from the experience learned in past farms A similar process indicates that it does not affect inflation in the long term. The decline in expectations inflation is apparently to a large extent a result of the appreciation that has increased in recent months, And I'll expand on that later. In contrast, among the forces acting to increase inflation are the following: The fact that the economy is approaching full employment and real wages are rising. As long as the price decline continued The inputs, employers could absorb the increase in wages without rising prices. This phenomenon was reflected in the gap that opens between the change in GDP prices and the change in consumer prices. However, this gap has begun to close, meaning that it is not expected to continue throughout. time, and then the increase in wages will translate into an increase in the cost of labor per unit of GDP that is expected to operate to the increase of inflation. An increase in inflation among our main trading partners is also expected To contribute to an increase in inflation in Israel. Indeed, despite the very low level of inflation expectations In the short term, medium-term and long-term expectations are within the target range, even if they were affected To some extent from the processes that are of a short-term nature. Monetary policy, however, It will continue to act in order to bring inflation to within the target range. National Accounts data for the fourth quarter were very strong, but they emphasized the need for informed analysis of the data that is published. The Bank of Israel's assessment is that a significant portion of the high growth in the fourth quarter was the result of Increased importation of vehicles in December, at a rate that cannot be assumed to continue throughout the year. Also minus This effect, the growth rate of the economy is satisfactory, and the indicators available to us now point to for the fact that this pace apparently continued in the first quarter of 2017 as well (although it is possible that the growth figure that will be published about it will be low due to the same volatility in vehicle imports). The labor market continues to demonstrate Power; The increase in real wages continues, and the participation and employment rates are stable at a high level. continuation The decline in unemployment, with the stability of the job vacancy rate at a relatively high level, may To indicate that there has been a further decline in structural unemployment in the economy. The picture that emerges from the data on the economy The world is a bit more optimistic than the one we have seen so far. Indicators of activity in the main economies were Positives: There was an improvement in the growth rate of world trade, there were price increases in equity markets in Europe and emerging markets, and the increase Inflation in most economies continued. In the US, the recovery in activity and the entrenchment Inflation near the target led the Fuded to raise the interest rate again, but The future interest rate path that emerged from the forecasts of senior FeD officials still reflects accommodative policy, a sign that the recovery still needs policy support. Accommodative monetary. In addition, there is still uncertainty regarding the administration's economic policy. New. In Europe as well, the recovery is in its shadow of political uncertainty, although this diminished slightly after the election results in the Netherlands. With that, for now, the ECBcontinues its very accommodative monetary policy. The fact that even in emerging markets, a trend is becoming apparent An improvement may indicate the beginning of a global trend of recovery. If it happens, and if The risks to the continued growth of world trade as a result of the political processes will not be realized, it will be Good news for the land of Israel as well. In the effective exchange rate, the appreciation continues and is amounted to 3.1 percent in the fourth quarter, and despite the widening of the interest rate gap vis-a-vis the US, there was An appreciation of 4.5 percent against the dollar as well. Part of the appreciation reflects the relatively good state of the economy The Israeli one, which is reflected, for example, in the current account surplus and in the relatively high growth. However, In our assessment, the sharp appreciation that occurred in recent months was partly an overvaluation, reflecting, among other things. the very accommodative policy adopted by some central banks. In this context, it should be emphasized that In the US, despite an interest rate increase, the Fedis still repurchasing assets Against those he has purchased in the past and are coming to maturity. transition The fact that the appreciation postpones the entry of inflation into the target range, the overappreciation has a negative impact on industries the tradable sector in a way that may be irreversible; For example, when the temporary factors that cause are exhausted The overvaluation, those enterprises that could not exist at the level of the exchange rate that is appreciated in the redundancy did not will be able to return to activity even though they have the right to exist in the exchange rate that represents equilibrium. Therefore, in addition to the low interest rate, the Bank of Israel sometimes intervenes in the foreign exchange market. It is of greater intensity when, in the Monetary Committee's assessment, the discrepancy between the fluctuations in the exchange rate The actual exchange and those derived from the basic forces in the market is greater. I will emphasize again, as I also noted here three months ago, that there is no ceiling for the foreign exchange reserves, and the Monetary Committee You will be able to operate in the foreign exchange market to the extent that monetary policy needs dictate it. Although a number of demand and supply factors have moved in the direction which should have caused a cooling off in the housing market, and the last two observations indicate stabilization Some prices are still too early to conclude that the increase Prices have been halted. The monthly rate of new mortgages taken out continues to decline against the background of an increase in the interest rate Mortgages and building starts maintained a high pace in 2016, and there was also an acceleration in building completions data. certainly, and the number of transactions is reduced. The government is making considerable efforts to continue increasing supply The apartments and it is important that you stick to this. The macroeconomic staff forecast presented by the Research Department to the Monetary Committee and published today to the public (which, as we recall, is a conditional forecast based on assumptions about the exogenous variables), reflects the division's assessment according to which the anomalous effect of Vehicle imports on growth in 2016 are not expected to continue in 2017, when growth is expected at a rate of 2.8%; However, at the basic growth ratethat is, Net of the fluctuations resulting from vehicle imports--only a moderate decline is expected, with a change in composition Growth: The growth rate in private consumption is expected to moderate, while a recovery in exports is expected Given that the improvement in world trade will continue. This growth composition is expected to prevail in 2018 as well, when it is expected Growth of 3.3%. The path of the interest rate and inflation that emerge from the forecast are lower than those in the forecast The previous one, mainly due to the effect of the appreciation that occurred in the shekel: Inflation is expected to enter into the target only in the second half of 2018, and the first increase in the interest rate is expected only in the second quarter of 2018. In conclusion, monetary policy continues to operate To return inflation to within the target range, to offset the overvaluation of the shekel, and to support the future Growth. To date, the effect of the relatively sharp appreciation and the changes in consumer behavior and competition In the economy on inflation, stronger than the effect of wage increases and higher inflation worldwide, so that despite the continued increase in inflation over the past year, it is still expected to continue to be Below the target for more than a year. Therefore, as I noted at the beginning of my remarks, the Monetary Committee intends to keep the policy that is already accommodative, as long as necessary in order to entrench the inflation environment within the target range. Happy holiday.

Title: Remarks at a meeting of the Knesset Reforms Committee on increasing competition in the banking market
text: Remarks by the Governor at a meeting of the Knesset Reforms Committee on the approval of a bill to increase competition in the banking market in Israel 06/09/2016 Corneal Flug A little over a year ago, the Minister of Finance and myself established a committee to examine increasing competition in the financial system (the Strum Committee). The task was not simple, and it took a long time, mainly due to the complexity of the financial system, the complexity of the recommendations, and the technological changes that are sometimes faster than the pace at which policy makers formulate the recommendations. It also took a lot of work to translate the recommendations into a bill that would faithfully reflect the committee's recommendations. I would like to commend all the partners, members of the Strum Committee, representatives of the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Justice, the Antitrust Authority, and representatives of the Bank of Israel, who managed to formulate recommendations for the benefit of consumers while maintaining the stability of the system. I think that changes in financial systems, due to their complexity and their impact on the entire economy, are important to be made by agreement based on the assessments of the professional bodies, and the bottom line is that we have reached such agreements. The changes set out in the law, and in particular, the recommendation to separate the two credit card companies from the large banks, alongside initiatives led by the Bank of Israel and the Banking Supervision Department, such as building a credit database, an outline for establishing new banks from the ground up, promoting efficiency in the banking system, and advancing technology and innovation in the banking sector, will create in the coming years an advanced, and more competitive banking system in the retail and small business sectors. It should be remembered, however, that a change in the financial system requires informed, thorough, and long-term measures, and requires a little patiencethe fruits of the reform will be reaped by the public gradually, over time. In this regard, it is important that during the transition period, customers holding credit cards will not be harmed, so we thought it would be appropriate for the banks to reduce their credit facilities to customers over 4 years and not over two years, since in our opinion, the credit card companies are unable to absorb in two years a volume of facilities that are greater than the total number of facilities they currently provide. Neither in terms of the scope of their sources nor in terms of capabilities related to risk management. Another area that occupies a significant part of the committee's recommendations is the area of payment systems. In this area as well, and in part as a continuation of the Committee's recommendations, the Bank of Israel has recently led significant changes that will increase competition in this area, including the opening of the Shva protocol and the establishment of access conditions for payment systems, which will remove barriers and enable the entry of new players into various segments of the system, and will support the development of innovative and advanced means of payment. As for the risks inherent in the reform, it should be noted two main risks that we will have to deal with: one, more banks, more small banks, and more non-bank financial intermediaries mean a higher risk of a financial intermediary collapsing; And the second risk is thetrend of rapid expansion of credit to households. Therefore, it is important that increasing competition in the credit market, which is important in itself, be done cautiously, while paying attention to the developing risksand with proper supervisionof the new credit providers. The Financial Stability Committee, whose memorandum of law on the matter was published about two months ago, and which will institutionalize the cooperation and coordination between the various regulators on the financial system, will have an important role in ensuring the monitoring, early identification, and timely handling of risks to the financial system. Against the background of the expected changes in the financial system, it is even more important to complete the legislation for its establishment as soon as possible. Another point in the prudential aspect relates to the supervision of entities that issue bonds and provide credit at the same time. Just a year ago, an amendment to the Banking Licensing Law was approved, which set a threshold of NIS 2.5 billion, above which supervision will remain in the hands of the Bank of Israel. There is great importance in maintaining such regulatory status, since at such volumes there is growing concern for the stability of the financial system in the event of a failure of these companies, and therefore there is room for prudential supervision similar to the supervision that exists over banking entities. Another complementary and necessary step is to promote and improve the tools for dealing with a bank in difficulties and a failed bank, including deposit insurance. These tools, which have become very common throughout the world, inter alia after understanding the lessons from the financial crisis, will provide a safety net in case a bank enters into difficulties, so that the damage to depositors, the financial system, and the economy will be moderate. I can guarantee that all the many steps we take in the field of competition are done responsibly, after a serious and professional examination of the possible benefits and risks arising from each and every step, and this is a critical condition for the success of the measures for consumer welfare while minimizing the risks that exist in the process. In conclusion, the measures in the bill will lead to a fundamental change in the degree of competition in the financial system. It is important now to focus on the implementation of the reforms, and to give them time to influence. These are great changes and we must also allow the system to adapt to them, and reach the new equilibrium that will be created as a result of the changes and reforms. Another word to conclude, I do not need to explain to the honorable members here the responsibility placed on you to issue legislation that will ultimately serve the public in the best possible way. Professional knowledge at the Bank of Israel was an important component in formulating the Strum Committee's recommendations, and I would like to offer you, members of the Committee, the Bank of Israel's professional assistance in this important legislative process as well.

Title: Remarks at the Al-Qasemi Business Conference 2016 on trends and challenges in the Israeli economy
text: Remarks by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel at the Al-Qasemi Business Conference 2016: "Trends and Challenges in the Israeli Economy" 07/12/2016 Baudot-Trajtenberg Nadine Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Dr. Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg spoke today at the Al-Qasemi Business Conference at the Al-Qasemi College of Engineering and Science in Baqa Algarvia. Following are the main points of the Deputy Governor's remarks:  The macroeconomic data of the Israeli economy are relatively good relative to the global environment.  The labor market continues to show strength: the unemployment rate is lowand the job vacancy to unemployed ratio is steadily increasing.  Israel is fertile ground for innovation and high-tech: the expenditure on research and development in Israel and the investment in venture capital are among the highest in the world.  Alongside the positive picture conveyed by macro data, there are challenges facing the economy, chief among them the highest poverty rates among the advanced economies.  There are gaps in skills and achievements in the field of education between the various populations in Israel and between Israel and the developed countries, as indicated by the results of the PIACC survey, the TIMSStests, and the PISAtests published this week.  In Arab society lies a significant part of Israel's future growth potential:For example, the banking system has identified this potential so that in the past decade, the number of branches serving Arab society has almost doubled.  Improving skills and achievements in Arab society will contribute to accelerating the economy's growth rate. In order for this to happen, we need to increase the number of male Arab students, and to integrate Arab female students in quantitative fields of study as well. Dr. Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg emphasized that "the great economic challenges of the Israeli economy also lie in the great opportunities it faces: on the one hand, the level of GDP per capita in Israel, which is an indicator of a lower standard of living than in most OECD countries, joins the high rates of poverty and inequality in which the economy is characterized. On the other hand, this starting point allows us to increase the growth rate by increasing the skills and quality of education for all citizens, in a way that will maximize the human capital resource, especially in Arab society. The demographic trends and the potential for investment in human capital open up an opportunity for Israel to generate rapid and robust growth, an opportunity reserved for few developed countries. While the world continues to slowly recover from the crisis, Israel enjoys a healthy macroeconomic environment that enables it to address the economy's long-term challenges. We will not be able to escape the responsibility for the future by evading it in the present, we must act"

Title: Remarks at a meeting of the Knesset Finance Committee on virtual currencies
text: Remarks by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel at a meeting of the Knesset Finance Committee on the activity and use of virtual currencies 08/01/2018 Baudot-Trajtenberg Nadine Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Dr. Nadine Baudot-Trajtenberg addressed a number of issues and issues in the context of the virtual currency phenomenon at a meeting of the Knesset Finance Committee this morning. Following are the main points of her remarks: The virtual currencies that exist today are based on private initiatives and no official body, such as central banks or governments, stands behind them. Against the background of the great interest in the purchase of virtual currencies, especially by young people, it is very important that anyone considering this be aware that this is an activity for which there is no government responsibility, and that they take into account that the high volatility and lack of supervision may lead to a sudden loss of value. Bitcoin and similar virtual currencies are neither a currency nor are they considered foreign currencies  the Bank of Israel's position is that they should be viewed as a financial asset, with all that this implies. As part of the functions assigned to the Bank of Israel in the Bank of Israel Lawto issue the official currency that is legal tender in Israel and to regulate the cash system in the economythe law defines the currencythe "New Shekel." As part of the Bank of Israel's functions to manage the foreign exchange reserves and to monitor developments in the foreign exchange market, the law also defines "foreign currency" as "banknotes or coins that are legal tender in a foreign country and are not legal tender in Israel." If so, Bitcoin and similar currencies do not meet the legal definition of currency or foreign currency. Beyond the legal definition, even when considering the economic parameters of virtual currencies, they do not fulfill the main functions of a currency. A critical element that exists in the currency is the degree of trust that users place in it. This confidence stems from the fact that money is a legal tender with legal backing and fulfills its generally accepted qualities according to the economic literature - an accounting unit, an instrument for conducting barter, and a stability that allows it to be an instrument for maintaining value - all of which do not exist in Bitcoin and similar currencies, which are characterized by extremely high volatility, difficulty in carrying out transactions, and lack of confidence regarding the factors behind them. Recently, there have been a number of complaints among the public about alleged difficulties that banks place on customers who wish to transfer funds from their bank accounts for the purpose of purchasing virtual currencies. Beyond the risks to the customer, there are also compliance risks for the bank. It is important to illustrate: the anonymous nature of virtual currencies means that they can be used, and are used, for money laundering, crime financing, and the like. A customer who wishes to transfer his money to any stock exchange that sells virtual currencies can later transfer the money anonymously to any dubious entity in Israel or around the world. If the money will be used For an improper purpose, the bank that made the transfer may be liable against law enforcement authorities in Israel or abroad. Therefore, each bank is required to define whether it provides services to customers in this area, and if so, how it will manage the risks. The Banking Supervision Department's directives require the banks to take precautions to prevent money laundering and the financing of terrorist activity, and to comply with the rules of the International Task Force (FATF). Thus, there are signs that require banks to treat customers' accounts as high-risk accounts. One of the signs is a large cash activity. In this regard, the transfer of virtual currency is equivalent to the transfer of cash and therefore the account can be considered one with high risk. The Banking Supervision Department has established an internal team to examine and study the issue, And he is at the beginning of work. It should be noted that it is not possible to learn much from what exists in the world, since, as far as we know, no regulator in the world has issued a directive to the banking system on how to act with regard to customers' activity in virtual currencies. Our assessment is that this indicates that there is a real difficulty in providing sweeping guidelines to the system regarding the correct way to estimate, manage, and monitor the risks inherent in this activity. Therefore, at this stage, the Banking Supervision Department cannot provide a response to customers whose banks refuse to allow them to convert the money in their accounts into virtual currencies. If a solution is found, it will have to be provided jointly with the Israel Money Laundering and Terror Financing Prohibition Authority and be acceptable to it.

Title: Lecture: "Monetary Policy in an Era of Low Inflation"
text: Lecture by Andrew Abir, Director of the Bank of Israel's Markets Department: "Monetary Policy in an Era of Low Inflation". 08/02/2018 Andrew Knight Monetary policy and inflation Andrew Abir, Director of the Bank of Israel's Markets Department, lectured today at the IBI Investment House, and discussed the monetary policy conducted by the Bank of Israel in the era of low inflation. Abir mentioned the Bank of Israel's objectives as defined in the Bank of Israel Law, and the tools through which it is possible to act to achieve these goals. The main tool, of course, is the interest rate, which has been at a low level of 0.1 percent since 2015, in view of the decline in inflation to below the target range of 13 percent. Abir mentioned, While the Fed has begun a gradual process of raising interest rates, several central banks, led by the ECB, are even adopting a policy of negative interest rates. While the interest rate affects short-term yields, other tools can affect long-term bond yields: the Bank of Israel, like other central banks, uses "forward guidance," and other central banks have adopted, and some are still pursuing, a policy of purchasing bonds, which significantly increased their balance sheets. Another tool is intervention in the foreign exchange market, which also contributes to increasing the central bank's balance sheet. In January 2018, the Bank of Israel intervened in the market on a significant scale, inter alia after the market identified considerable activity in the sale of foreign currency according to models. The significant intervention halted the appreciation, despite the marked weakening of the dollar against major world currencies. Is monetary policy succeeding in achieving its targets? The labor market is at full employment and the economy is growing in line with its potential growth rate. The main transmission mechanism of monetary policy to real activity has been operating in recent years mainly through the effect of the policy on private consumption, which led growth. The inflation environment, however, is still below the target. Part of the decline in inflation reflects "imports" of low inflation from abroad, which, together with the effect of the appreciation, leads to a decline in the prices of tradable goods. In Israel, inflation has also been affected by government initiated price reductions, and structural changes that increase competition in the economy are acting to reduce inflation. These are desirable changes that affect the level of prices, and monetary policy does not attempt to act against them, or to offset them. However, a prolonged decline in the inflation rate to below the target may have negative effects on economic activity over time, and therefore the Bank of Israel's monetary policy is expected to remain accommodative, as long as necessary in order to entrench the inflation environment within the target range. Abir referred to the gaps in consumption price levels between Israel and the OECD countries, and noted that there is a high correlation between the level of the real exchange rate and the price gap: At the present time, the shekel is appreciated, and therefore the price level in Israel is high relative to abroad, since the appreciation reduces prices abroad in shekel terms more than in the domestic economy, where it affects only the prices of tradable goods. Real depreciation may narrow the price gap, As it was, for example, in the middle of the previous decade.

Title: Remarks by the Governor, Prof. Amir Yaron, at a farewell event for outgoing Supervisor of Banks Yair Avidan
text: Remarks by the Governor, Prof. Amir Yaron, at a farewell event for outgoing Supervisor of Banks Yair Avidan Yair, for the past 3 years, has led the Banking Supervision Department with professionalism, creativity and great dedication. Your extensive economic knowledge, combined with your rich experience in the banking world, was reflected in the way you led the Banking Supervision Department, and were an asset to Israel Bank. 12/06/2023 To view the speech as a file click here Hello everyone, Yair, I will begin by thanking you for your great work during the significant and challenging period that characterized your term. You began your position as Supervisor of Banks in the shadow of the COVID-19 crisis, at a time when there was great uncertainty and the financial system was turbulent. The vast experience and high capabilities with which you came to the position helped stabilize and advance the system. During your tenure, the Banking Supervision Department promoted a variety of measures to improve digitization and innovation in the payment and banking worlds, and to promote values of fairness and fairness. Thus, for example, in the area of consumer welfare, the Banking Supervision Department was a central player in the mortgage transparency reform, and in the interest rate transparency reform, in which comparative information on deposit and credit interest rates was published. In the field of financial stability and risk management, the division under your leadership dealt with global challenges such as COVID-19, the ramifications of the climate crisis, the war between Russia and Ukraine, examining the impact of rising interest rates on mortgage repayments, strengthening the level of protection and cybersecurity, and more. The Division has also not spared dealing with the issue of competition in the banking system. Suffice it to mention the open banking project, moving from bank to bank with a click, accompanying the establishment of a digital bank, granting a license for another digital bank, and more. These are, of course, only a taste in a nutshell of some of the measures that the Banking Supervision Department has escorted, initiated, and promoted as part of the goals of the Department and the Bank in general. All this under your leadership. Beyond your ability to work hard and outstanding achievements, you brought with you to the job a cohesive worldview and an orderly vision, and worked intensively and consistently to realize this vision - a fairer, more efficient, and more technological banking system. During your tenure, you have worked extensively on environmental and climate risks and on strengthening the banking system's activity in the ESG world. Just today, we published principles for effective management of climate-related financial risks. The directive will determine how the banks should act in order to manage their exposure to these risks, and is the result of intensive work by various entities in the Bank over a long period of time. It is evident that the issue is burning within you, and that you have managed to "pass the germ" to your subordinates. Yair, I think that there is no one in the hall who has not heard from you the words "fairness and fairness" that represent the way the banking system should treat its customers. In this regard, I think there has been some improvement in recent times. A number of banks have embarked on various programs designed to make it easier for their customers to cope with the challenging economic environment these days, and this is a welcome phenomenon. At the same time, your successor also has more work to do there are many layers in which it is possible to improve the dimension of fairness and fairness in the banking system. The banking system's profits are at record highs, deriving mainly from credit indexation mechanisms, large current account balances, and partial transmission of interest on deposits. All these are reflected in high interest spreads. I have told the editorial representatives who are with us in the past that I expect to see a higher transmission to deposit interest, and an active appeal to customers who have high balances in non-interest-bearing current accounts. A situation has arisen in which the banking system is the beneficiary of the fruits of the high interest rate, while the burden accompanying it rests on the shoulders of the financial consumer. To the extent that the increase in bank margin is higher than the increase in the risk environment, this is unfair and unfair. From a strategic perspective, this reality is also liable to undermine the legal and regulatory equilibrium in which the banking system currently operates. It is enough to listen to the various bills on banking that come up on a regular basis. The banking system must act wisely and intelligently to find a new, more correct and fair balance in the relationship between it and the financial customer, both because this is the right thing to do, and from a long-term strategic perspective. This is also the place to congratulate Danny Khakhiashvili, who is currently assuming the position of Supervisor of Banks. Danny has served in a wide range of positions at the Bank of Israel over the past 20 years, and he is starting his position at a time when various reforms to increase competition in the financial system, which we have worked on at the Bank of Israel in recent years, are beginning to come to fruition. Now it is necessary to make sure that the poet's intention is realized, and that the benefits to consumers - the public - will trickle down. At the same time, we see what is happening in the banking sector around the world and the importance of the stability of the banks and the financial system, which unfortunately is sometimes undervalued in certain regions. Danny, there's a lot of talk about "supervisor-supervised relations." There is no doubt that healthy and good working relations between the regulator and the supervised entities are of great importance. I think that Yair's personality, pleasantness and experience contributed significantly to building trust and cooperation with the banking system. Yair, for the past 3 years, has led the Banking Supervision Department with professionalism, creativity and great dedication. Your extensive economic knowledge, combined with your rich experience in the banking world, was reflected in the way you led the Banking Supervision Department, and were an asset to Israel Bank. In my opinion, the quality that is most significant in your role is your leadership ability. The appreciation that all your employees hold for you, without exception, is a testament to the person you are and your significant place in each and every one of them. In my experience, the interpersonal moments are precisely the ones that are most strongly etched in us, and you have countless of them. As for the near future - take advantage of the time to spend with your family, grandchildren and relatives, and for the distant future - I believe that you will find a way to contribute from the rich experience you have acquired at the Bank to the Israel economy and the challenges you have faced. I will conclude with your permission with thanks and best wishes to Yair's immediate family. In recent years, Yair has devoted most of his hours to working at the bank, 24/7. So from here I wish you - Liora, the children, the grandchildren - to enjoy Yair as much as possible and thank you for the period in which you "lent" him to the public service at Bank Israel. Thank you.

Title: Remarks by the Governor at the Interior and Environmental Protection Committee
text: Remarks by the Governor at the Interior and Environmen Protection Committee Bank of Israel Governor Prof. Amir Yaron spoke at the Interior and Environmental Protection Comi Bank of Israel Governor Prof. Amir Yaron spoke at the Interior and Environmental Protection Committee.
