Title: Pension Policy in Israel
text: Pension Policy in Israel 27/12/2007 Welfare Policy and Labor Market Pension Policy in Israel The main points from the Deputy Governor's lecture to the Sapir Forum, December 2007 Pension savings in Israel are particularly low among the lower deciles, the self-employed, those working in small businesses, temporary workers, and those employed part-time. However, for low-wage workers, it is not certain that saving for retirement is worthwhile. Increasing the cost of employing low-wage Israeli workers (up to NIS 4,500) by charging pension savings (particularly those employed in jobs requiring low skills and a short period of study) will increase the demand for employment of foreign workers  legal and illegal, to whom the increase does not apply. Therefore, applying a "compulsory pension" arrangement to Israeli employees requires regulation  for example, by increasing the cost of employment  and reducing the number of legal and illegal foreign workers. Requiring low-income earners whose wages are close to the old-age pension level to save for retirement will make it difficult to smooth the consumption over life and will harm their well-being precisely during the working periods, when the household includes a higher number of persons and a lower per capita income. Therefore, as part of the pension savings charge, it would be correct to set a minimum wage level above which the savings will apply.

Title: The importance of internal auditing in public bodies - the main points of remarks at the Internal Auditors Conference
text: The importance of internal auditing in public bodies - the main points of the Deputy Governor's remarks at the Internal Auditors Conference 31/12/2007 Bank of Israel - General 31.12.2007 The importance of internal auditing in public bodies The main points from the lecture of the Deputy Governor and Chairman of the Bank of Israel's Audit Committee Internal Auditors Conference, December 27, 2007 Internal auditing in state and public bodies contributes to streamlining work processes, saving resources and increasing transparency in the management of the organization. It also assists in the early detection of crises and risks at the organizational level and in the prevention and exposure of corruption and violations of procedures and laws. Tightening regulation on the internal audits of public companies will contribute to increasing investors' confidence in the robustness of companies and reducing financial risks in the economy. In order to ensure that the audit is carried out  and at an appropriate level  it is important to report on the performance of an internal audit to supervisory bodies, to determine indicators of the scope, quality and outputs of the audit, to supervise compliance with these indicators, and to supervise the identity and training of the auditors. "Handsome demands  handsome upholds": what is happening at the Bank of Israel? The Bank of Israel's internal audit includes an internal auditor with independent status and seven standards for internal auditors, five of which are currently staffed by professional auditors. According to the Internal Audit Law, the Bank of Israel's internal auditor is subordinate to the Governor of the Bank. However, in light of the importance of the audit, an audit committee headed by the Deputy Governor was established in 2006, consisting of three external and two internal members  although there is no legal obligation to do so. The Audit Committee at the Bank of Israel is working to correct deficiencies that arose in the State Comptroller's reportsas required by the State Comptroller's Law, discussing the findings of the internal audit reports, discussing the proposal of the annual work plan of the internal audit, and recommending it to the Governor. The Audit Committee at the Bank of Israel contributes to the efficiency and quality of the audit work and assists in maintaining its independence.

Title: Protection of Apartment Buyers - Following the Heftziba Affair
text: Protection of apartment buyers - following the Heftziba affair" 02/01/2008 Hizkiyahu Roni The Banking System 2.1.2008 "Protection of apartment buyers - following the Heftziba affair" The main points from the Supervisor of Banks' lecture, Mr. Roni Hezekiah, at a conference held at the Netanya Academic College The Supervisor of Banks, Mr. Roni Hezekiah, spoke at a conference held at the Netanya Academic College on the topic of "Protection of Homebuyers  Following the Heftziba Affair" on January 1, 2008. In his remarks, the Supervisor of Banks reviewed his extensive activity in providing assistance to buyers by issuing instructions to the banks to issue to buyers who meet the criteria he formulated, guarantees under the Sales Law, as part of the handling of hundreds of complaints from buyers. The Banking Supervision Department required the banks in those cases in which there was a failure in the process of depositing the funds or transferring mortgage funds to the loan account, to deposit funds into the escort account and to issue guarantees to the buyers. The issuance of guarantees is aimed at ensuring the investments of Heftziba buyers. In his remarks, the Supervisor emphasized that most of the projects are in advanced intermediate stages and the construction can be completed and the apartments can be handed over to the buyers, while minimizing the damage caused to the buyers due to the continuation of the proceedings. The Supervisor of Banks called for the completion of the projects to be made possible, while examining each project as an independent unit, which will lead to a solution to the distress of the vast majority of Heftziba buyers. In his remarks, the Supervisor of Banks referred to the solutions that he is formulating as part of the lessons learned following the Heftziba affair, including: a method that will ensure a deposit into the escort account and secure the buyers' funds while reducing the risks of fraud on the part of the contractor; and extensive public information regarding the protection of its rights in the process of purchasing the apartment. Title: The desired size of the government in Israel: the US or Scandinavia?
text: The desired size of the government in Israel: the US or Scandinavia? 17/01/2008 Strawczynski Michel Fiscal policy 15.1.2008 The desired size of the government in Israel: the US or Scandinavia? The main points were made by Dr. Michel Strawczynski, Deputy Director of the Research Department at the Bank of Israel, in a panel discussion organized by the Falk Institute The adoption of an annual goal of increasing public expenditure acted as a successful anchor for macroeconomic policy in Israel. The Scandinavian countries, which are characterized by a high share of public expenditure in GDP, have also recently adopted such rules. Decisions that the government has already made in the areas of education and welfare increase the real growth rate of expenditure in the budget to 2.53.0 percent. If the government does not cut expenditures in other areas, it will have to decide how to change the fiscal targets, in a way that will allow the continued convergence of the share of public debt in GDP to international standards. Despite the adoption of targets to stimulate the employment of workers from the lowest quintile, total government expenditure to encourage employment declined from 0.26 percent of GDP in 2006 to 0.21 percent in 2007. An examination of the fiscal rules in Israel, beginning in 1992, shows that replacing the deficit reduction law with a fiscal rule based on the annual growth rate of public expenditure has so far been a successful policy step. This is because, from a historical perspective, public expenditure is the engine of the dynamics of the additional fiscal variables in Israel (the tax rate, the deficit rate, and the debt rate). The recognition of the importance of public expenditure as an anchor for fiscal policy led to the fact that even the Scandinavian countries (Finland, Sweden, and Denmark), which are characterized by a high share of public expenditure in GDP, began to establish rules based on the growth rate of public expenditure. In 2007, Israel was characterized by a level of public expenditure equal to the average in Europe, while in 2000 the share of public expenditure in Israel was similar to that of Finland. In the multiyear budget recently published by the Bank of Israel's Research Department, it was determined that the most recent decisions made by the government in the areas of education and welfare have budgetary implications for an increase in government expenditure at a rate between 2.5 and 3 percent per year until 2010. If the tax reduction plan is implemented verbatim, the public debt is expected to decline to about 60 percent of GDP by 2016. This decline is liable to be delayed if it turns out that the growth in the economy's GDP will be lower as a result of the apparent slowdown in the US. Dr. Strawczynski also addressed the new goals of increasing employment and increasing the income of the lowest quintile, which were adopted by the government during 2007. To this end, he presented estimates of government expenditure to encourage employment. These estimates show that in 2007 there was an underperformance of government expenditure in this area, with a decline in expenditure to encourage employment from 0.26 percent of GDP in 2006 to 0.21 percent in 2007. This is in contrast to expenditure of about 0.7 percent of GDP in OECD countries.

Title: A summary of remarks in the Knesset Finance Committee
text: A summary of the Governor's remarks in the Knesset Finance Committee 02/04/2008 Fisher Stanley The economy and economic activity 2.4.2008 A summary of the Governor's remarks in the Knesset Finance Committee I would like to open by thanking Karnit Flug and Michel Strawczynski, who led the writing of the annual report, as well as for the presentation that Karnit has now presented. The Israeli economy is currently dealing with a very complex situation. In the Western world, and especially in the United States, there is a major financial crisis, and one of the consequences of this is a significant slowdown in growth in the United States and subsequently in Europe and in the volume of world trade. There is no room for doubt: the Israeli economy will be affected by the slowdown in global growth. This is expected to apply in two ways: first, the financial impact, the effect of property, and the effect of changes in the capital market on real investments in the economy; Second, the decline in the United States' demand for imported products  including Israeli products. In other words, regardless of the strengthening of the shekel, exports from Israel to the US are expected to be negatively impacted, followed by a negative impact on the growth rate to which we have been accustomed since mid-2003: more than 5 percent per year. The important question is to what extent the Israeli economy will be harmed and to what extent wethe government, particularly the Ministry of Finance, and the Bank of Israelcan influence the extent of the damage. I have no doubt that the government and the Bank of Israel have the ability to minimize, as much as possible, these effects on the Israeli economy. And what is the macroeconomic policy required for this? The answer is a continuation of the path we have followed in recent years: First, a budgetary policy based on the targets setregarding expenditure and the deficitand aimed at continuing to reduce the high ratio of government debt in GDP, is a policy that contributes to the activity of the business sector as a factor leading the growth of the economy, and in the process, also contributes to strengthening the financial stability of the economy. I would like to note here the vital contribution of the Minister of Finance and his ministry in this matter. Their adherence to budgetary discipline, despite the pressures and difficulties, was critical to the continued growth of the economy and to the economic resilience of the State of Israel. I know from the ongoing conversations that I am holding with the Minister of Finance and the Director General of Finance, that the Ministry of Finance intends to continue doing so, with the support of the Prime Minister and the government as a whole, and this will be a significant factor in the continued success of the economy in the coming years. Second, the Bank of Israel will continue its interest rate policy, the main goal of which is to maintain price stability. And I will return to this topic in a little while. Third, those problematic focal points that hinder the business sector from developing and leading the economy forward must be dealt with structurally. One of the main focuses is the bureaucracy, including  and to a significant extent  in the field of land and real estate. The Bank of Israel's growth forecast for 2008 is 3.2 percent, and it is based on continued macroeconomic policy, as I described. While this is a lower growth forecast than in recent years, it is a higher growth forecast than the forecasts for the United States, Europe, and the entire Western world. We have a good chance of getting through the current period relatively successfully, that is, with relatively rapid growth, and it depends on usboth in terms of growth and in terms of continued financial stability in the economy, despite the crisis in the US and Europe. I will now return to the issue of the Bank of Israel's interest rate policy. I want to make it clear: The main objective of the Bank of Israel's interest rate policy continues, as it was in the past, to maintain price stability in the economy. At the same time, the Bank will act to contribute to the government's other economic goals, primarily growth and employment, and also to support the financial stability of the economy. This is so long as it does not harm the main targetprice stability. In the past month, the Bank of Israel has taken a number of steps that were unusualintervention in the foreign exchange market, which was, and will remain, we hope, a rare eventthe implementation of a long-term program aimed at increasing the foreign exchange reserves, and two interest rate reductions that accumulated to one percentage point. All these steps were consistent with the objectives, as I mentioned. They are consistent with the return of inflation to within the price stability target range this year, and are intended to support and strengthen the financial stability of the economyand increasing the reserves does indeed strengthen the stability of the economy. In this way, the Bank of Israel makes its main contribution to economic growth in 2008, as well as over time. Our approach in managing interest rate policy is flexible with respect to the inflation target. It is the accepted approach in the modern economy, it is the well-known and accepted approach in England, and it is the approach of any modern central bank operating within the framework of an inflation target. As I have described several times in the pastincluding in the publicit is also the approach to the Bank of Israel's inflation target. This perception of seeing the targets stems from the relative advantages of interest rate policy and is therefore reflected in the modern central banking concept, and therefore in the laws of central banks in advanced countries. This is also the perception that is reflected in the proposal for the new Bank of Israel Law that we are working on formulating, together with the Ministry of Finance, and with the support of the Prime Minister. This is a law that will meet the high standards of central banks in advanced countries. We hope to bring the new bill to the Knesset soon, thereby strengthening the legal infrastructure for an advanced and modern Bank of Israel that will be proud of the State of Israel and its citizens.

Title: The pressures to appreciate the exchange rate in the first third of 2008
text: The pressures to appreciate the exchange rate in the first third of 2008 18/06/2008 Assistant Balfour Foreign exchange market 18.6.2008 The pressures to appreciate the exchange rate in the first third of 2008 From the beginning of the year to the end of April, the shekel appreciated by about 11 percent against the dollar and by about 6 percent against the euro. The weighted rate of strengthening of world currencies against the dollar indicates that about half of the shekel's strengthening against the dollar during this period was influenced by global factorsthe weakening of the dollar worldwideand half by domestic factors. The main explanation for the domestic factors that acted on the exchange rate during this period lies in the development of the basic account in the balance of payments (the current account in the balance of payments and other long-term capital flows), and mainly a significant reduction in the inflows of capital going abroad by Israeli residents, against the background of the global financial crisis. According to the basic account data, which are presented in the attached table, the global financial crisis was not reflected in the incoming capital flows, because foreign investors continued to invest in Israel at a rapid pace similar to previous years. In contrast, the crisis affected Israeli residents, who greatly reduced the pace of their investments abroad, and nonresidents' investments in the economy totaled 16.5 billion in the first third of the year at an annual rate, compared with 12.4 billion in 2007. On the other hand, investments by Israeli residents abroad amounted to only 5.7 billion at an annual rate in the first third of the year, compared with 12.4 billion in 2019. As a result, in the first third of the year, there was a surplus of 10.8 billion, in annual terms, in long-term capital imports to the economy compared with a balance in imports last year. The table also shows that part of the underlying pressure for the appreciation of the exchange rate was offset this year by reducing the current account surplus. Thus, partial data on the current account for the first quarter of the year indicate that a reduction in the surplus accrued in 2007 is apparent. This is mainly against the background of the apparent slowdown in world trade, the upward trend in global energy and commodity prices, and the continued appreciation of the shekel. According to Bank of Israel estimates, the current account is expected to total a surplus of about 0.8 billion in the first quarter of the year, compared with a surplus of about 2 billion in the corresponding period last year, and in 2008 as a whole, a deficit of about 0.5 billion is expected, compared with a surplus of about 5 billion in 2008. The Bank of Israel's assessment is that the underlying pressure for the strengthening of the shekel is expected to moderate, and it is even possible that there will be a change of direction during the year. This is primarily as a result of the expected continued contraction of the current account surplus later in the year until a deficit is created, and as a result of foreign exchange purchases by the Bank of Israel with the aim of increasing the level of foreign exchange reserves, which are expected to total about 10 billion over the next two years. Moreover, if there is moderation in the global crisis, there may be a resumption of outgoing capital flows, mainly by institutional investors, which will add to the pressure to devalue the exchange rate. The Bank of Israel emphasizes that these assessments relate to the basic long-term pressure on the exchange rate, and they do not take into account the short-term pressure that depends on the interest rate differential and other factors. Therefore, these assessments should not be considered a forecast of the exchange rate.

Title: Remarks at the Economics Committee
text: A summary of the remarks made by the Supervisor of Banks, Mr. Roni Hezekiah, at the Economics Committee 17/06/2008 Hizkiyahu Roni The Banking System 17.6.2008 A summary of the remarks made by the Supervisor of Banks, Mr. Roni Hezekiah, today at the Economics Committee As a result of the reform's implementation, bank customers will save, in our assessment, about NIS 500 million a year; This is the amount of loss of revenue expected for the banks following the cancellation of fees and the reduction of tariffs according to the reform. 80 percent of bank customers in the household sector will already benefit from a marked reduction in banking services. This was even before the process of increasing competition began, following the reform. Later in the process, and as a result of it, customers are expected to enjoy additional discounts. The reform is already beginning to achieve its goal. Since the publication of its details, banks have begun to publish updated - discounted rates. The situation of the weaker populations, whose activities are characterized by a lack of access to electronic means, was improved following the reform, which increased their access to branch operations compared to the previous situation (four clerk actions per month at the cost of operating through a direct channel, instead of only two actions in the past). Reducing the fees to only two and other steps that the Banking Supervision Department has taken and will take enable the customer to know the cost of managing his account, an ability that he did not have before. The Banking Supervision Department welcomes the public and media involvement that arose as a result of the reform. Such involvement was not possible in the past, due to the inability to know and compare the prices of banking services. This is the beginning of the process of improving conditions for customers. The Supervisor of Banks emphasized that he intends to closely monitor the implementation of the reform, and that he will not hesitate to exercise the authority granted to him by law and intervene where necessary.

Title: Main points at the Naamat conference on women's integration into the labor market
text: The main points of Dr. Karnit Flug, Director of the Research Department at the Bank of Israel, at the Naamat conference on the integration of women into the labor market 23/09/2008 Corneal Flug Welfare Policy and Labor Market 22.9.2008 The main points of Dr. Karnit Flug, Director of the Research Department at the Bank of Israel , at the Naamat conference on the integration of women into the labor market The employment rate of women of prime working age in Israel (25-64) is similar to the average rate in OECD countries. However, the gaps between the employment rates of women from different population groups are very large: while the employment rate of Jewish women is relatively high  about 70%, those of Arab Israeli women are less than 30%. While the employment rates of educated women (13 years of schooling or more) are over 75%, those of women with less than 12 credits are less than 40%. Among the non-working women, of the main working ages, about two-thirds cited the care of children or the household as the main reason why they do not work, and also among those who work part-time voluntarily, a major reason for their choice to work part-time is the care of children. It is important to note that the fact of women's non-employment, or their partial employment, is reflected, among other things, in relatively high poverty rates in families with only one breadwinner. Studies point to the effectiveness of subsidizing daycare and preschool education as effective tools to encourage the employment of mothers. In light of these findings, and in light of the fact that the government's socioeconomic agenda focuses on reducing poverty by encouraging employment, it is important to find out to what extent the public system supports the creation of conditions that will encourage women to integrate into employment, and how it is possible to increase the incentives for women's integration into the labor market. In view of the high weight of childcare for reasons of non-employment, it is likely that the encouragement of employment should also focus, first and foremost, on improving accessibility, and reducing the cost of childcare. In February 2007, the government decided to increase, during the years 2008-2010, the budget for daycare centers by NIS 67 million annually. Consequently, both the number of children in public daycare centers and the subsidy rate increased considerably. However, even after this increase, the share of children aged 0-3 in public daycare centers is not high in Israel compared to other countries (about a quarter, but still significantly lower than in countries such as Denmark, Sweden, and Belgium, where the rates are much higher). One of the characteristics of government support for daycare centers is the progressiveness of the support, meaning that it is focused on low-income populations. However, despite this, among Arab Israeli women, the rates of eligibility for daycare centers are particularly low. Thus, while Jewish families receive a subsidy for about 15% of the children, Arab families receive subsidies for daycare centers for only 6% of the children, despite being represented at a very high rate in the low-income population. Pre-primary education, for ages 3-5, constitutes, beyond its contribution to child development, also an important element in encouraging women to go to work . Even in preschool education, public expenditure in Israel is relatively low (76% in Israel compared to 80% on average, in the OECD). In this area as well, the expansion of preschool education, especially in low-income areas, could contribute greatly to women's employment, thereby reducing gaps and poverty. It is important to note that when the state spends relatively little on caring for young children, private expenditure is a substitute for public expenditure. However, this is closely related to the family's economic income: while families in the lower third of the income distribution spent an average of about NIS 200 per month per child aged 0-5 per child, families in the upper third spent about NIS 1480 per month per child. These also express the differences in the employment hairs of women between the quintiles, but they, in themselves, intensify inequality. Another tool used by the state to encourage women's employment are the child credits for working mothers. However, this tool benefits high-income women, who are above the tax threshold and therefore can enjoy the benefit. It is important to note that 80% of mothers do not fully utilize the tax benefits. Half of them are not working, and half because their income is relatively low. In conclusion, it is worth emphasizing that the employment rates of women in disadvantaged populations are relatively low, contributing to poverty rates and high income gaps. Expanding the subsidies for daycare centers, daycare centers, and after-school programs, while focusing on low-income populations, including the Arab Israeli population, could help increase employment rates. The expansion of compulsory preschool education, especially in weaker areas, will also contribute to increased integration of women into the labor market. On the other hand, there is no room to expand tax benefits to working women as they increase the income of high-wage women whose employment rates are already high.

Title: Remarks at the Global Interdependence Center conference at the Hebrew University on the State of the Israeli Economy
text: Deputy Governor at the Global Interdependence Center conference at the Hebrew University: The financial crisis finds the Israeli economy in the best state since the establishment of the state; The recent interest rate reduction will lower the costs of credit to the business sector 03/11/2008 Eckstein Zvi Financial Markets and Financial Stability 3.11.2008 Deputy Governor at the Global Interdependence Center conference at the Hebrew University: The financial crisis finds the Israeli economy in the best shape since the establishment of the state; The recent interest rate reduction will lower the costs of credit to the business sector "The global financial crisis, the worst since 1930, finds the Israeli economy in its best state since the establishment of the State of Israel. Its ability to deal with crises stems to a large extent from the preservation of the budget framework by fiscal policy (public debt - 77.7% of GDP, public expenditure - 44% of GDP, deficit is 1.5% of GDP), and on price stability, which is achieved by monetary policy as well as the balance between imports and exports," said Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Prof. Zvi Eckstein today in a lecture he gave at the GIC conference at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. "Maintaining a stable economic policy contributes to social welfare in an economy that is exposed to the global economic shock, and is often in an economic crisis as a result of the security situation," Eckstein added. In his speech, Eckstein said that the Ministry of Finance, the Israel Securities Authority, and the Bank of Israel are closely monitoring developments in the financial markets in Israel and abroad. According to him, the market reaction in Israel is in line with global trends, but there was no need for significant intervention in Israeli markets. "The policy regarding the financial crisis is determined by the Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Israel after consulting with the professional teams," said Eckstein. Referring to the Bank of Israel Law, which is currently in advanced discussions between the Bank and the Ministry of Finance, Prof. Eckstein said that the enactment of a new Bank of Israel Law is essential for strengthening Israel's economic stability and its integration into the global economy. According to him, the legislation should be based on several principles: increasing the independence of the central bank in the management of policy and in the management of the bank; defining policy targets for the Bank, chiefly the price stability target, alongside sub-objectives such as supporting GDP and employment and maintaining the stability of the financial system; the establishment of a monetary committee and a management council; Increasing transparency and depth of reporting in the bank's conduct and management. In his remarks, Prof. Eckstein referred to the interest rate decision for November: "The reduction of the interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.50 percent is consistent in achieving the price stability target and supporting economic growth and financial stability. The worsening of the global crisis and its impact on the Israeli economy increased the chances of a slowdown in the growth rate in the coming period. Lowering the interest rate will support lowering the costs of credit to the business sector at this time."

Title: A summary of remarks today on a panel at the Prime Minister's Conference on Business
text: A summary of remarks by Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Prof. Zvika Eckstein today on a panel at the Prime Minister's Conference on Business 12/11/2008 The economy and economic activity 12.11.2008 A summary of remarks by Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Prof. Zvika Eckstein today on a panel at the Prime Minister's Conference on Business Advanced financial instruments are an essential and necessary part of efficiency, liquidity and competitiveness in financial systems around the world. What are these devices? 1. REPO for managing the financial flows of large financial entities and managing monetary policy 1.1. MBS, CDO and securitization of other cash flows (rental payments, capital notes, etc.) to liquidate assets as well as to divide yield and risk 1.2. CDS  Bond risk insurance and risk transfer between institutions and between different points in time 1.3. Wright Funds 1.4. Monetary funds and monetary funds for payments 1.5. All these instruments are today in the headlines of the financial crisis. The volumes of trading in them have recently grown in the world to enormous proportions. Some of them were also traded at prices that did not match the risk, and some of them became incomprehensible due to excessive complexity and lack of transparency and institutional responsibility. 2. These instruments cannot be used without the formulation of appropriate rules in the following areas: property and pledge laws, taxation of capital gains, supervisory provisions on procedures and capital allocations, accounting, transparency and disclosure rules, and the existence of supervisory coverage of all the institutions involved. 3. The current financial crisis (similar to previous crises) is due, to a considerable extent, to failures in the regulatory rules of these instruments, but also to a lack of understanding by the market of the probabilities of the various risks. Why? 4. These instruments significantly reduce the costs of the total or partial transfer of assets, between individuals or institutions (banks, insurance companies, funds, funds, etc.) 5. Laws, instructions, and rules are like signs, traffic lights, and car traffic lines that mark who is driving, where, when, and at what speed. Without these rules, the markets are dysfunctional and if you drive too fast the accident can be quite brutal. This seems to be the case, but even those who walk may be partially affected. 6. The current crisis is partly too fast driving on unmarked roads. Or risk prices that are too low and liquidity  the ability to transfer assets  is fast and cheap without proper scrutiny. 7. Here  in Israel  these financial instruments have not been developed at all. We didn't attend the celebration so we don't suffer from hangovers. Still, in order to be part of the global financial world, a sophisticated, efficient capital market must be developed that efficiently allocates capital in savings and investments  we must develop the new financial instruments. 8. What we are doing today is building the entire range of laws, directives, taxes, etc. in accordance with what has been learned from the crisis in various countries so that in Israel these financial tools will develop efficiently and safely. The repo market rules are over and only the clearing house should be opened and the tax legislation in the Knesset should be completed. We will open securitization over the next few months, as will the other issues, at a pace and order that will suit the efficiency and competitiveness that will not harm financial stability. 9.

Title: Summary of Lecture at the Aaron Banking Center - Bar-Ilan University
text: The Financial Markets in Israel: A Snapshot and a Look to the Future, Summary of Prof. Eckstein's Lecture at the Aaron Banking Center - Bar-Ilan University 16/07/2008 Eckstein Zvi Financial Markets and Financial Stability The Financial Markets in Israel: A Snapshot and a Look to the Future, Summary of Prof. Eckstein's Lecture at the Aaron Banking Center - Bar-Ilan University Summary: The current financial crisis broke out after almost a decade of relative quiet, and after several years in which risk prices, that is, the spreads between risky and non-risky ratios, were very small. Most of those involved in analyzing international financial markets note that this is the most complex and difficult crisis since the crisis of the 1930sthe "great depression." Background  The importance of financial markets The financial markets are where savings are allocated: people decide where to save, but financial institutions manage their savings. These entities use savings to provide credit, which they give to various entities based on considerations of return and risk. Credit recipients invest it, thereby driving the economy's growth process. A key component of the financial markets is the payment systems. The security and efficiency of these systems depends on the functioning of the markets, and hence their importance for economic growth. The regulator is entrusted with regulating the market. The development of the financial markets over the past two hundred years would not have been possible without institutional regulation of these marketsof the payment systems, of credit risk control, and of managing residents' savings. The financial markets have often been in the eye of the storm of financial crisesas they are today. Hence the utmost importance of creating transparent and effective rules to promote their efficiency, competition and stability.

Title: The main points of remarks at the "New Financial Order" conference  TheMarker's conference of economic experts
text: The main points of remarks by Deputy Governor Prof. Zvika Eckstein at the "New Financial Order" conference  TheMarker's conference of economic experts 08/12/2008 Financial Markets and Financial Stability 08.12.2008 The main points of remarks by Deputy Governor Prof. Zvika Eckstein at the "New Financial Order" conference - The Marker's Conference of Economic Experts "The financial crisis that is currently plaguing the global economy finds the Israeli economy in excellent macroeconomic conditions: the debt to GDP ratio, the share of expenditure from GDP, and the deficit are at levels that support stability. Confidence in monetary policy is high, and long-term inflation expectations are anchored around the midpoint of the inflation target range. A balance prevails between imports and exports, and the current account is in excess. The capital to balance sheet ratio in the banking system is between 11 percent and 12 percent, and the state of the credit portfolio is very good. Few are the countries whose economic situation during this crisis is so good. In Israel, therefore, no dramatic steps were required as those taken in the US and Europe." This is what Prof. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, said today at the "New Financial Order" conference at the Tel Aviv Exhibition Center. "However", noted Prof. Eckstein, "the Israeli economy is part of the global economy: 45% of production is intended for export; Israelis raise capital in Israel and invest it abroad; Large Israeli companies operate directly abroad, and their assets abroad reach the level of GDP in Israel; Foreigners own assets in Israel. Therefore, the response of Israeli capital markets to the crisis is essentially similar to the reactions of capital markets around the world. Israel is not an island of stability but a stable ship in a raging sea." Against this background, Prof. Zvi Eckstein noted the two main issues on which government policy should focus: Increasing inventory and reducing the cost of credit available to financial entities and allocating it to small and medium-sized businesses. Special allocation is required for exporting businesses. All this through the banks as well as in new funds that will be established. A. Policy that supports employment: Due to the slowdown in demand for workers and the increased risks of layoffs and business closures, some of which are already being realized, steps should be taken to encourage the employment of the unemployed and the "negative income tax" and "lights to employment" programs should be expanded.

Title: The main points of remarks at his lecture at Intel
text: The main points of remarks by Dr. Michel Strawczynski, Director of the Macropolicy Division at the Bank of Israel Research Department, in his lecture at Intel 10/12/2008 Strawczynski Michel 10.12.2008 The main points of Dr. Michel Strawczynski's remarks, Director of the Macropolicy Department at the Bank of Israel Research Department, in his lecture at Intel The recession in the US began in early 2008, but hit Israeli high-tech exports in the third quarter of the year. The relatively late response stems from the nature of this recession: unlike the recession that prevailed in the US in 2001, which initially focused on the high-tech industries, the current recession began in other sectors of the US economy, primarily the housing market. In terms of the adverse impact on employment, there is a marked difference between the various industries in the economy: so far the manufacturing industries have been negatively impacted, while in other sectors, such as transportation and communications, the increase in employment has continued. While in the US and Europe a further decline in GDP is predicted in the last quarter of 2008, in Israel it is projected that for the first time after five years of continuous growth, GDP will not increase. The team for diagnosing U.S. business cycles officially determined at the end of Novemberbased on employment, income, and production datathat the boom in activity ended in December 2007, and therefore the U.S. economy has been in recession since the beginning of 2008. In contrast to the crisis of 2001, which initially focused on the high-tech industries, this time the source of the crisis is in other sectors of the economy, mainly in the housing market. The decline in demand abroad had a negative impact on exports of manufacturing industries in the third quarter, particularly in high technology industries. According to the Labor Force Survey for the third quarter, the number of those employed in manufacturing has already declined, and it appears that there will be a further decline in the last quarter. However, the picture is not uniform in all industries: thus, in the transportation and communications industries, there was a solid increase in employment in the third quarter. According to the new OECD forecast, further declines in GDP in the US and Europe are expected in the last quarter of 2008 and in the first two quarters of 2009. These will affect Israel's high-tech exports, and therefore, for the first time after five years of continuous growth, we expect that GDP in the last quarter of 2008 will not increase. The extent of the negative impact on exports of high-tech industries in Israel will depend on the recovery of the US economy. The recovery in the US is expected, according to the new OECD forecast in the third quarter of 2009. This is assuming that there will be a "soft landing" in fiscal policy, including a reduction in the medium term (between 2 and 5 years) of the budget deficit that has prevailed in the US economy for several years. In accordance with current decisions, the cyclically adjusted deficit in the US is expected to increase from 1 percent in 2007 to 3 percent in 2008, and to remain at this high level in 2009 and 2010 as well. This deficit means a continued increase in the US public debt, and OECD economists note that reducing it in the future is an important condition for returning to a path of sustainable growth.

Title: Remarks at the conference "The Israeli Economy and the Financial Markets in the Wake of the Crisis"
text: Deputy Governor at the conference "The Israeli Economy and the Financial Markets in the Wake of the Crisis A Look to the Future"  a symposium in memory of the late Prof. Shmuel Kandel at Tel Aviv University 19/01/2009 Eckstein Zvi Financial Markets and Financial Stability 19.01.2009 The Deputy Governor at the conference "The Israeli Economy and the Financial Markets in the Wake of the Crisis A Look to the Future"  a symposium in memory of the late Prof. Shmuel Kandel at Tel Aviv University "The financial crisis is leading to a significant recession of economic activity in the Western world and a sharp decline in growth in developing countries. The financial crisis in the US and Europe is being intensively handled by governments, central banks, and various supervisory bodies. We hope that during 2009 these policy measures will bear fruit, and that the money and credit markets will return to functioning, so that the necessary conditions for resuming global economic growth will be created. The policy measures in the real sphere are intended to reduce the adverse impact on activity, but cannot prevent it." This is what Prof. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, said today at the conference "The Israeli Economy and the Financial Markets in the Wake of the Crisis: A Look to the Future," a symposium in memory of the late Prof. Shmuel Kandel at Tel Aviv University. "The Israeli economy entered the crisis under excellent macroeconomic conditions," added Prof. Eckstein. "We ended 2008 with a debt-to-GDP ratio, a share of expenditure from GDP, and a deficit at low levels that support stability. Confidence in monetary policy is high, and long-term inflation expectations are anchored in the central boundary of the inflation target range. There is a balance between imports and exports and a surplus in the current account. Capital adequacy in the banking system is good, although not high by international comparison, and the financial system is stable. Although the stock and credit markets reacted to the crisis similarly to most markets around the world, thanks to the stability of the banking system and other financial institutions, no dramatic steps were required similar to those taken in the US and Europe." Prof. Eckstein noted that the negative impact on the Israeli economy, like other small economies, derives from the exposure of exportsthe main growth engine in recent yearsto a dramatic decline in demand abroad. The decline in activity lowers tax receipts, so in 2009 a significant increase in the deficit is expected. In order to maintain the stability of the economy and prevent a further increase in the price of credit, the government should not be allowed much freedom in increasing expenditure that will lead to an increase in the debt to GDP ratio. In addition, Prof. Eckstein added that the Bank of Israel has adopted a policy of lowering the interest rate in order to minimize as much as possible the costs of credit to the business sector and to meet the inflation target under these conditions. Prof. Eckstein described the necessary government measures that need to be taken immediately in order to expand the credit inventory and lower the increases: immediate activation of the guarantees program for the banks in order to enable them to raise capital, a significant expansion of the guarantees program for small and medium-sized businesses, and a special Arab program for institutional investors. In addition to accelerating activity in the field of infrastructure, land must be released and plans for construction must be promoted. In addition, R&D support should be significantly expanded, in order to encourage innovation ahead of the exit from the crisis and to maintain the most skilled workforce in the exporting industries. In order to meet the budgetary constraints, most of the expenditures are manageable, but adjustments in the budget may be required. In Prof. Eckstein's assessment, preparations should be made in a few months to improve the financial systems in Israel by strengthening supervision of financial risks. This is done by transferring supervision of the financial risks of the entire economy to the direct management of the Bank of Israel. It is also necessary to monitor and implement changes taken in the financial systems in the Western world. In addition, the development of financial markets should be carefully promoted through strict regulation of securitization of flows of receipts of banks and other entities and the elimination of tax distortions. The operation of the repo market in Israel this year - noted Prof. Eckstein - is a welcome step in this direction.

Title: Remarks at the conference on "Development of the Financial Markets and Regulation due to the Crisis"
text: Supervisor of Banks Roni Hezekiah spoke today at a conference on "Development of the Financial Markets and Regulation due to the Crisis," held at the Interdisciplinary Center Herzliya. 30/03/2009 Hizkiyahu Roni The Banking System 30.3.2009 A summary of the remarks made by Supervisor of Banks Roni Hezekiah at a conference held today at the Interdisciplinary Center (IDC) in Herzliya Supervisor of Banks Roni Hezekiah spoke today at a conference on "Development of the Financial Markets and Regulation due to the Crisis," held at the Interdisciplinary Center Herzliya. The Supervisor addressed the challenges of financial regulation and the first insights from the development of the global crisis in Israel and around the world. According to him, financial regulation in Israel should move from an institutional (sectoral) supervisory structure to a goal-oriented (functional) supervisory structure by way of uniting supervisory authorities. In addition, the Supervisor emphasized the importance of unifying prudential supervision at the Bank of Israel in view of the lessons learned from the global crisis by supervisory authorities around the world. The Supervisor added that against the background of the development of the global crisis, a trend of full or partial unification of supervisory authorities is identified around the world, while expanding the central bank's preoccupation with the stability of the financial system and individual financial institutions. The central bank's involvement in issues of stability is essential both for effective handling of the crisis and for the prevention of a crisis. Another emphasis placed around the world is the need for a high level of coordination and cooperation between the supervisory authorities and between them and the Central Bank to achieve supervisory efficiency. In Israel, there is a sectoral division between 3 supervisory authorities according to types of institutions: the Banking Supervision Department at the Bank of Israel, the Capital Market, Insurance and Savings Department of the Ministry of Finance, and the Israel Securities Authority. The Israeli economy is characterized as a small economy with high concentration in banking and insurance. In recent years, there has been a trend of blurring the boundaries of the activity of the various financial entities, including credit activity and activity in the securities market, and these and other changes emphasize the need for an overall view of the financial system and maintaining its stability, while achieving maximum coordination between supervisors and emphasizing the application of equitable regulation and supervision to the financial entities. The transition from sectoral supervision to functional supervision and the unification of prudential supervision at the Bank of Israel will make it possible to achieve these objectives, while adapting to the structure of the financial system, achieving efficiency and flexibility in the implementation of supervision, and ensuring the status and ability of the Banking Supervision Department in dealing with crises.

Title: Remarks at the Annual Conference of the Israel Bar Association on Government Intervention and Deposit Insurance
text: Prof. Zvi Eckstein at the Annual Conference of the Israel Bar Association: A clear, transparent and consistent policy is needed for government intervention and deposit insurance for individuals and businesses, especially for the large financial entities 01/06/2009 Eckstein Zvi The economy and economic activity 1.6.2009 Bank of Israel Deputy Governor: There is a need to create, in international coordination, clear and uniform rules for supervising financial institutions, particularly the world's largest banks Prof. Zvi Eckstein at the Annual Conference of the Israel Bar Association: A clear, transparent and consistent policy is needed for government intervention and deposit insurance for individuals and businesses, especially for the large financial entities "The global financial crisis is reflected in the decline in the value of the world's largest financial institutions and in the spillover into all the financial and real systems in the various countries. This crisis is essentially the result of an over-expansion of consumer debt and corporate debt in the U.S.debts included in the assets of the largest banks in the UK and several other countries. The financial stability control systems in the US and other countries, which were supposed to prevent such a development, failed - similar to the failure in past crises, especially in the great crisis of 1929-33." This is what Prof. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, said today at a conference of the Israel Bar Association held in Eilat. Prof. Eckstein spoke on the panel "Banking Law - Real Estate Crisis and Financial Crisis". "The monetary policy currently being pursued in Israel and abroad," added Prof. Eckstein, "is in line with the findings of the studies of leading economists and is also being implemented in the inflation target policy in Israel. In such a major financial crisis, maximum monetary accommodation should be adopted, which includes lowering the central bank's interest rate as much as possible, buying government bonds, and even actions by the central bank as a "lender of last resort" in order to stabilize the financial markets. The economic models give us a framework of thinking and action that has proven to this day to be effective, understandable and traceable in a world of business cycles. This policy has been successful even during the crisis, and is reflected in a marked decline in credit costs and in the maintenance of medium-term inflation expectations both in Israel and around the world around the midpoint of inflation targets." Prof. Eckstein said that in the field of financial stability and supervision, no cohesive framework has been created in the world for anti-cyclical policy, which prevents over-inflated household and business debts, and clearly and consistently handles large entities during a crisis. It is necessary to create, in international coordination, a framework of clear and uniform rules for the supervision of financial institutions, and in particular of the largest banks around the world. A clear, transparent, and traceable policy is needed for government intervention and deposit insurance for individuals and businesses, especially for the large financial entities. In this context, Prof. Eckstein noted that the Banking Supervision Department's policy in Israel functioned adequately during the crisis. Prof. Eckstein mentioned that the budgets of many countries, including Israel, have entered into heavy deficits, mainly due to a significant decline in tax revenues, but also due to an increase in government spending. If a credible policy of reducing government debts around the world is not outlinedas is the case in Israelwe are liable to find ourselves in prolonged macroeconomic instability. For the time being, it appears that the policy of financial stabilization in the US, and to a large extent in Europe, is building confidence, and that the markets are returning to regular activity. If, toward the end of the year, government involvement declines, and the stabilization of the financial markets becomes entrenched, we can expect a resumption of growth in the US as early as the first quarter of 2010, and subsequently in Europe as well. This growth will also make it possible to renew the growth of Israeli exports, and with it  of the entire economy. The challenge facing monetary policy in Israel and abroad is to respond even before the data on renewed growth are certainin order to prevent a marked deviation of inflation above its target.

Title: Remarks at the Caesarea Forum on Budgetary Reduction and Taxation
text: Deputy Governor at the Caesarea Forum: Interest payments and high defense expenditures do not allow for budgetary reduction, and therefore there is no room for lowering taxes, beyond the levels budgeted in the budgets for 2009 and 2010, which will lead to a further increase in the debt burden 01/07/2009 Eckstein Zvi The economy and economic activity 30.6.2009 Deputy Governor at the Caesarea Forum: Interest payments and high defense expenditures do not allow for budgetary reduction, and therefore there is no room for lowering taxes, beyond the levels budgeted in the budgets for 2009 and 2010, which will lead to a further increase in the debt burden. Prof. Zvi Eckstein: "The focus should be on reforms that will streamline the public apparatus in the Israel Lands Administration, in ports and in the electricity sector" The relative size of the government and the composition of public expenditure affect economic growth. The main mechanisms for this impact are, among other things, public expenditure on research and development, investment in infrastructure and human capital, employment rates, and the quality and efficiency of the bureaucracy, said Prof. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, in a panel titled "The Desired Size of the Government  Between Economics and Politics" at the Caesarea Forum, which is being held in Eilat. Eckstein added that in recent years, the size of the budget in Israel is similar to the average level in OECD countries, with the business sector becoming a dominant growth engine in the economy. However, interest payments on debt and defense spending in Israel are still significantly higher than in other advanced economies: interest payments on debt to GDP in Israel are more than 3 percent higher than in the eurozone and the US, and defense spending is also significantly higher. The result of the high expenditures, with components that do not encourage growth, is low investment in infrastructure and education, which harms growth. In addition, in the quality of regulation, bureaucracy and public service to the business sector, according to 11 international rankings, Israel is on average in 35th place, which is extremely low. According to Eckstein, a significant part of the public sector's activity does not optimally support economic growth and its ability to reduce gaps vis-a-vis other developed economies and to be one of the most developed economies in the world. Given the budgetary constraints, he said, the focus today should be on reforms that will streamline the public apparatus, such as the reform of the Israel Lands Administration, the ports, and the electricity sector. Eckstein: "The high interest payments and defense expenditures do not allow for budgetary reduction, and therefore there is no room for lowering taxes beyond the levels budgeted in the 2009 and 2010 budgets, which will lead to a further increase in the debt burden."

Title: Remarks at Ben-Gurion University
text: Remarks yesterday by Prof. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, at Ben-Gurion University 08/12/2009 Eckstein Zvi The economy and economic activity 08.12.2009 Remarks yesterday by Prof. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, at Ben-Gurion University "The main problem in the financial markets in Israel is in the financing of non-bank credit to real estate by institutional investors and the public", saidProf. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, in a lecture at Ben-Gurion University. "This problem," he added, "requires adjustments in the areas of supervision of nonbank credit." Prof. Eckstein noted that the aforementioned problem is not directly related to the "Bachar reform", which contributed to the improvement of the capital market by reducing conflicts of interest between savers and money managers, increasing supervision of savings consulting, and increasing transparency and competitiveness in managing individuals' savings. Referring to monetary policy, Eckstein added that the pace of interest rate increases in Israel, in the process of emerging from the crisis, will be based on the need to maintain price stability within the inflation target range of 13 percent. This is so that inflation will be, as far as possible, near the midpoint of the target range of 2 percent. He argued that monetary policy would continue to support economic growth and employment, as long as this goal did not contradict achieving the inflation target over time. Prof. Eckstein went on to discuss the Bank of Israel Law, which is currently due to reach the Knesset, and emphasized the importance of the law for establishing the stability and growth of the economy: "The Bank of Israel Law will strengthen the anchoring of inflation and inflation expectations around the target set by the government (1 to 3 percent), will anchor the Bank's policy support for employment and growth in a way that does not harm the price stability target over time, and will anchor policy support in financial stability. The existence of an independent administrative council with powers in the areas of management, and a monetary committee with powers in the field of policy decisions, will improve the quality of the Bank's management and decision-making. This will ensure the public an efficient, transparent public body with a high international status."

Title: Summary of Remarks at the Annual Executive Conference of the Israel Management Center
text: A summary of the remarks made today by Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Prof. Zvika Eckstein before the annual executive conference of the Israel Management Center 26/01/2010 Eckstein Zvi The economy and economic activity 26.01.2010 A summary of the remarks made today by Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Prof. Zvika Eckstein before the annual executive conference of the Israel Management Center Bank of Israel Deputy Governor: "Israel has been better at getting through the crisis than most advanced economies" "Israel has been better at getting through the global crisis than most developed countries. This is due to several key components that characterized the Israeli economy prior to and during the crisis," said Prof. Zvi Eckstein, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, in a lecture he gave to the annual board of directors of the Israel Defense Forces (IMC). Flexible monetary policy with an inflation target (13 percent) and a willingness to intervene in the financial markets when they deviate from conduct that is consistent with basic economic conditions. Responsible and conservative policy of the Banking Supervision Department, which focuses on the risks of the loan and money markets. Balanced fiscal policy combined with a low debt-to-GDP ratio (77 percent)a policy based on automatic stabilizers, that is, on increasing the deficit through a decrease in taxation and not through a system of incentives that increases the public expenditure base. A significant surplus in the current account, exports rich in advanced technologies and attractiveness of the Israeli economy among foreign and domestic investors. "The main weaknesses of the economy, which we must deal with the day after the crisis," Prof. Eckstein added, "are the low productivity in the non-exporting industriesthe services, finance, and public sectorsand the high inequality in household income." Inequality is reflected in a high poverty rate, resulting from low employment rates, low wages in low-skilled jobs, and a limited system of welfare services for the weaker populations. Prof. Eckstein went on to discuss the challenges of fiscal policy, and emphasized that investment in Israel, relative to GDP, in health services, infrastructure, welfare services, and employment-supporting services is among the lowest in the developed countries. "After the public expenditure on interest and defense was subtracted," he added, "the volume of public expenditure in Israel is low relative to other economies." According to Prof. Eckstein, in order to ensure sustainable growth, we must deal with the challenges of the education system and maintain a declining debt-to-GDP ratio, we must reconsider the path of tax cuts, and maintain, in the 2011 budget, the current size of expenditure relative to GDP.

Title: Remarks at the session on "Reducing Socioeconomic Gaps as a Component of National Resilience"
text: Remarks by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel today at the session "Reducing socioeconomic gaps as a component of national resilience" at the Herzliya Conference 09/02/2011 Eckstein Zvi Welfare Policy and Labor Market 09.02.2011 Remarks by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel today at the session "Reducing socioeconomic gaps as a component of national resilience" at the Herzliya Conference Bank of Israel Deputy Governor Prof. Zvi Eckstein presented today the main points of the policy paper of a think tank headed by him that was submitted to the eleventh Herzliya conference. The paper presents the reduction of economic gaps, social integration, and the advancement of populations of low socioeconomic status as a strategic goal for the State of Israel. At the beginning of his remarks, Eckstein emphasized that addressing the issues of gaps requires consistent, multidimensional, continuous and long-term treatment. A necessary condition for this is the stability of the economy, which is supported by budgetary credibility that has been achieved in Israel in recent years. The headlines today that demand a populist policy response of tax cuts as a response to price increases and an increase in the minimum wage by several months may undermine the credibility of fiscal policy, and therefore these changes should be postponed, especially since these measures divert attention from a real and consistent handling of the problems of socioeconomic disparities. Eckstein emphasized that the headlines in the press are largely the result of the government not investing enough in long-term handling of this issue. The Deputy Governor noted that the main problem facing policy in this area is the increase in gaps in employment, income, and human capital, which leads to a weakening of social resilience and a negative impact on economic growth. The policy should focus on increasing employment and income from work by increasing the human capital of populations from low socioeconomic backgrounds. To do this, measures must be taken to promote the skill level of disadvantaged populations. The education system should focus on imparting skills in areas such as linguistic literacy and scientific and technological writing, computer use, business entrepreneurship, financial markets, economics and accounting, etc. An infrastructure should be created for the integration of students into the employment system (industry, commerce, services, and public), for example, by creating guidance centers for high school graduates. The Deputy Governor mentioned the targets set by the government in the area of employment: increasing the employment rate for working ages from 70% today to 76% in 2020, which will be reflected in all sectors, particularly among Arab Israeli women and Haredi men, which will lead to an addition of 33,000 workers annually beyond the natural growth in the labor force, and an increase of 0.5-1% in GDP growth; and reducing poverty so that the increase in income of the lowest quintile will be 10 percent greater than the increase in median income by 2020, which will lead to a real addition of 27 percent to family income and reduce the incidence of poverty by one percentage point. Prof. Eckstein listed the tools that can be used to achieve the goals: the establishment of guidance centers, training and incentives for special populations; increased enforcement of labor laws, particularly the Minimum Wage Law and the employment of foreign workers without a permit; preventing discrimination and affirmative action for special populations; making academic studies accessible to haredim and Arab Israelis; daycare centers in the Arab sector; the creation of a public transport infrastructure subsidized and adapted to employment; and the national application of negative income tax. The implementation of these programs, with the possibility of expanding and deepening them, will enable the economy to embark on a path of reducing gaps and economic growth based on increased employment and income of populations of low socioeconomic status.

Title: The main points of remarks at the Falk Institute symposium at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem on 29 May 2011
text: The main points of Dr. Michel Strawczynski's remarks at the Falk Institute symposium at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem on 29 May 2011 30/05/2011 Strawczynski Michel Fiscal policy 30.05.2011 The main points of Dr. Michel Strawczynski's remarks at the Falk Institute symposium at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem on 29 May 2011 Following are the main points of Dr. Michel Strawczynski's remarks at the Falk Institute symposium at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem on 29 May 2011: Meeting the deficit targets in recent years has contributed to the Israeli economy's successful handling of the economic crisis that has befallen the world. Against the background of the uncertainty created by the geopolitical changes that may affect defense spending, it is important to avoid worsening the budget imbalance starting in 2013. During the crisis, the economy managed to lower the share of public debt to GDP, while many countries increased their debt, making it difficult for them to recover from the economic crisis. The strategy of keeping the deficit low in the period preceding the crisis, and the aspiration to gradually reduce the share of the public deficit in GDP after it, proved to be very successful; This is what Dr. Michel Strawczynski, deputy director of the Research Department, said today at a conference of the Falk Institute on "Priorities in the Government Budget." The events taking place in Arab countries are liable to affect the geopolitical balances that exist today, although it is still too early to determine what kind of impact the events will have in the long term. In the short term, the events are likely to affect the development of actual defense expenditure in Israel, which is different from the original budget, after several years in which defense expenditure increased on average by about NIS 2 billion per year (Figure 1). It should also be noted that in recent years, the actual expenditure in the defense budget was higher than the original budget. Dr. Strawczynski argued that it is important that any budgetary decision made in the coming months, including those related to wage agreements, takes into account the expected impact of the decision on the government budget in the coming yearsand particularly starting in 2013: according to the Research Department's forecasts and based on the decisions made so far, the deficit is expected to be 3 percent of GDPabove the target set for that year, which is 1.5 percent of GDP. This estimate does not include the salary agreement with the secondary school teachers (signed yesterday) and with the doctors (which is being negotiated). Given that civilian expenditure in Israel (as a percentage of GDP) is relatively low relative to OECD countries, and particularly given the need to continue investing in education, the degrees of freedom of future policy scenarios are limitedand they require looking at all the components of fiscal policyincluding tax revenues. As noted, a future downward path of income tax rates for individuals and corporate tax has been set. As of today, it appears that it will be possible to implement the plan while maintaining the deficit targets only if the growth rate in the economy is significantly higher and over time than the forecastat a rate above 5 percent per year. It should be emphasized that in the past year, the growth rate has indeed been at this pace, and if it continues like this, it will be possible to implement the plan. At the same time, the uncertainty regarding growth and the notable advantages of reducing the debt, as mentioned above, make it necessary to consider among the alternative decisions facing the government. Title: Lecture at the Israel Democracy Institute: Lines for the Image of the Middle Class
text: Lecture by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel at the Israel Democracy Institute: Lines for the Image of the Middle Class 21/03/2012 Corneal Flug Welfare Policy and Labor Market 21.03.2012 Lecture by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel at the Israel Democracy Institute: Lines for the image of the middle class Dr. Karnit Flug: "The approval of the criteria for affordable housing as recommended by the Trajtenberg Committee should be promoted" In the past decade, the real income of the middle class has risen just as much as the increase in GDP per capita; The income of the lower class lagged significantly behind per capita GDP growth; The income of the upper classes increased faster than the growth of GDP per capita Between 1997 and 2010, the real income of the middle class increased by about 20%, and from 2007 to 2010 by 4%; The largest expenses for families with young children: housing and education Last summer's social protests brought the situation of the middle class into public debate. However, until recently, there was no clear identification and characterization of the middle class in Israel, and in any case, the question of how its situation has changed over time has not been examined. As part of the work on the Bank of Israel's report, which is due to be published at the end of the month, a few days ago the Bank of Israel published a paper with a detailed characterization of the middle class, which also describes how its situation has changed over the past 15 years. At a seminar held at the Israel Democracy Institute, Dr. Karnit Flug, Deputy Governor of the Bank of Israel, presented lines for the image of the middle class in Israel. The middle class is defined as the population of households whose income (adjusted for family size) is between 75% and 125% of the median income. According to this definition, the middle class constitutes about 27% of households, similar to its share of the population in 1997, while the share of the lower class expanded slightly, to 41%, and that of the upper class declined slightly, to 11%. 88% of middle-class households are non-Haredi Jews, about 9% are Arabs, and less than 3% are Haredi. Within the Arab population, 80% are from the lower class, and only about 15% are from the middle class. Within the Haredi population, 81% are from the lower class, and only about 13% are from the middle class.the composition of the middle class household is varied: about half are couples with 1-4 children (most of them 1-2 children), almost 30% are singles or couples without children, and another 15% are elderly. Most of the heads of households in the middle class have a post-secondary education (53%), but there are also more than a third who have 11-12 years of schooling. The lion's share of the income of middle-class households, about 85%, constitutes income from labor, and about 9% from allowances and subsidies.Looking over time, the real (net) income of middle-class households has increased over the past decade, just as the increase in GDP per capita, meaning that the fruits of growth have also permeated the middle class. In contrast, the income of the lower class lagged significantly behind per capita GDP growth, while the income of the higher classes increased faster than per capita GDP growth. These developments have been reflected in a marked increase in inequality over the past decade. In terms of the development of the income of middle-class households compared to the development of the prices of the consumption basket, it appears that from 1997 to 2010, the real income of the middle class (i.e., income minus the increase in prices) increased by about 20%, and from 2007 to 2010 by 4%. Although certain expenditure items, such as electricity, gas, and water, as well as fuel and transportation, became more expensive quickly, at the same time other items (such as clothing and footwear) were relatively reduced. In terms of the expenditure burden out of household income, it appears that in families withyoung children, the burden of expenditure on a mortgage or rent is significant. The rate of expenditure on a mortgage or rent out of the income of the middle class is 17% and 18%, respectively, and in the lower class 29% and 34%, respectively. Expenditure on caring for young children is also significant as a share of income: expenditure on education in middle-class families with young children (up to age 9) accounts for about 11% of their income. Therefore, the Trajtenberg Committee chose to focus on this population group, and on these two components of expenditure. In this framework, the government has already approved the main recommendations in the field of early childhood care (free education for ages 3-4, expanding the availability and subsidization of daycare centers, and subsidizing after-school programs), and the test will, of course, be implemented. The proposals to expand the supply of apartments, including affordable housing and long-term rental housing, have also been approved by the government, and I hope that the criteria for eligibility for affordable housing as formulated by the Trajtenberg Committee, which include maximizing earning capacity (125% of the position), will also be approved. The implementation of all of these, alongside the addition of tax credit points for fathers of young children, will make a significant contribution to improving the welfare of young working families, during a period in their lives whose earning capacity is still low, and the expenses, particularly on housing and childcare, are high.

Title: Remarks by the Supervisor to the Gala Evening - "Impact  the Growth Engine of the Future"
text: Remarks by the Supervisor to the Gala Evening - "Impact - the Growth Engine of the Future" Supervisor of Banks Yair Avidan spoke at the Rothschild Foundation Gala 14/03/2023 To view this announcement as a file click here The Supervisor of Banks, Mr. Yair Avidan, spoke at the Rothschild Foundation Gala, following are his remarks: Good evening I cannot begin my remarks as Supervisor of Banks without referring to the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in the United States and noting that we are closely examining the case and its implications. In addition, we are of course monitoring continued developments in the US banking system. These developments represent an important opportunity to emphasize what is taken for granted by many, and for us in the Banking Supervision Department is the bread of our laws - ensuring the stability and strength of the banking system in Israel. The stability of the banking system and credit card companies has greatly assisted the Israeli economy in weathering significant economic crises, and its readiness to overcome challenging economic scenarios is constantly being tested by us. And of course, the stability of the banking system has a direct interface with public trust and consumer welfare, and has a direct impact and contribution on future economic growth. I will now move with your permission to the reason for our exciting gathering today. I will begin my remarks with a quote from Hillel the Elder from Tractate Avot chapter 1, Mishnah 14: "If I don't have me, who am I. And when I'm to myself, what am I. And if not now, when." In the short code words, Hillel the Elder outlined a person's responsibility to himself, to the society in which he lives, and the short time available to him. A person must take responsibility for his own destiny, he must initiate and act with determination to improve his living conditions and his world. It is activity rather than passivity, initiative rather than reliance on others, that will lead to achievements. However, the individual cannot reach his full potential without being assisted by, contributing to, and contributing to the society in which he lives, contributes and contributes to it at the same time. If a person feels that he must do something right and proper, there is no reason for him to postpone doing it in the long term, but it is important to act here and now. I came to my position as Supervisor of Banks about three years ago out of a sense of mission, to do everything I can so that we will live here in a better society.
