The beginning of my job was accompanied by the COVID-19 crisis, which demonstrated even more strongly the fragility of life, and the connectivity of all systems: health, social and economic. The crisis has also helped us focus on our weaknesses as a society: the elderly, the weaker strata, the multitude of diverse sectors with unique characteristics, and made it clear to us that we, as a society, are as strong as the weakest link. The Bank of Israel, including the Banking Supervision Department, are institutions characterized by policy-making and long-term thinking. Therefore, alongside concern for stability, we are working to instill social responsibility thinking and encourage the banking system to see itself as a partner in shapingthe socioeconomic fabric of the economy and society and to maximize the good of all stakeholders - to increase value for customers, invest in employees, conduct themselves ethically and fairly, support the community and protect the environment. That is, to implement what is commonly called "attentive capitalism." I firmly believe that profitability achieved through the creation of environmental or social value has a higher strategic value than "old world" profitability. In this context, Harvard University has developed the concept of "shared value" over the past decade. Behind this concept is the notion that to remain competitive in today's world, companies need to do more than just monetize. They need to create shared value, that is, to create economic value in a way that also addresses social or environmental needs, bringing about a profound change in strategic thinking and business model. Through this conceptual shift, businesses differentiate themselves, open new paths of growth for themselves, and also achieve better bottom lines. From a business perspective, creating "shared value" is a way to gain a significant competitive advantage. At the same time, a shared value can "make the pie bigger", which is an important value in itself. Alongside the shared value, it is no less important to mention the company's purpose, a purpose that should correspond and take into account all stakeholders. The Banking Supervision Department has acted quite a bit in recent years to strengthen socioeconomic resilience. In this context, I will note: Regulating the field of corporate responsibility disclosure In December 2021, the Banking Supervision Department published amendments to the Supervisor of Banks' Public Reporting Directives, which are intended to improve the disclosure given to the public by banking corporations on environmental, social, and governance aspects. These amendments are part of the steps taken by the Banking Supervision Department to strengthen the banking system's contribution to the environment and society, thereby strengthening the long-term sustainability of the banking system and the economy, in accordance with the experience accumulated in the banking system in Israel and banks around the world in disclosing these issues. Addressing climate risks There is broad agreement around the world that the climate crisis, like the COVID-19 crisis, stems from a failure that cannot be solved only by market forces and therefore requires government involvement. Central banks and supervisors responsible for financial stability also have a significant role to play in this matter, but it is important to understand that the activity of financial regulators is complementary and cannot replace the activity required of governments. The Banking Supervision Department is currently formulating an up-to-date and comprehensive banking directive on climate risk management, based on the recommendations of the Basel Committee. This is a principle-based directive, which will deal, inter alia, with aspects of corporate governance, internal controls, establishing a risk management framework and conducting scenario analysis. The draft directive has been forwarded to the supervised bodies, and the aim is to publish a final directive in the first half of 2023. In the meantime, the Supervisor's letters sent to the banks require them to identify, assess and manage environmental risks in accordance with emerging standards around the world. Promoting Financial Availability Charter to Address Economic Violence This is a voluntary treaty, in which focused financial support is provided and the needs of victims of violence are met through domestic violence treatment centers, shelters and transitional apartments. The financial system works to provide victims of violence with financial guidance and guidance, in order to assist them in their first steps to economic independence, after their world has changed radically. The convention also includes additional measures designed to help victims of violence disconnect from their previous lives and financial dependence on their spouse. This charter was formulated and is being promoted by the Banking Supervision Department and the Association of Banks, together with the Ministry of Social Affairs and Social Services, banks, credit card companies, the Postal Bank, the associations that operate shelters for women victims of violence, and various social organizations. This year, the Convention was extended to survivors of prostitution and we hope that it will have a beneficial impact on their rehabilitation. Promoting a Charter to Make Banking Services Accessible to Senior Citizens In order to assist senior citizens in Israel with the challenges created in obtaining various banking services against the background of the COVID-19 pandemic, in December 2020, the Banking Supervision Department, the Ministry of Social Equality, the Association of Banks, and the Banking System formulated a voluntary charter to make banking services accessible to senior citizens. As part of the agreement, it was agreed that each bank would provide various alternatives for making banking services accessible through a mobile branch, improving the telephone response provided to senior citizens, priority in service, informational materials on digital conduct, and more. Promoting gender equality in the composition of the board of directors in the banking system In April 2022, the Banking Supervision Department published an amendment to the directive on board composition, which aims to diversify the gender composition on the boards of directors of supervised corporations, in order to ensure appropriate representation of both sexes. The amendment allows women to take a more active role in shaping strategies that integrate a broader range of opinions, perceptions and values, and to exercise influence in the decision-making centers of supervised corporations. Activities to increase financial awareness in Arab society The Banking Supervision Department leads various activities every year, in cooperation with the banking system and the Association of Banks, as part of a financial education forum, whose goal is to increase financial awareness among various populations in Israeli society, inter alia for the purpose of reducing information gaps, familiarizing the public with its rights, and obtaining tools for creating change for optimal financial conduct. As every year, these activities are held in a uniform format and without marketing marks, for the benefit of the citizens of the country. Over the past few years, the content has been dedicated to senior citizens, households, youth and more. In the past year, extensive activity was carried out in June and December, through the Financial Education Forum, to increase financial awareness in Arab society, which took place in dozens of localities throughout the country and with the participation of thousands of customers of the banking system. The participants received tailored lectures in Arabic on a variety of topics including balancing income and expenses, means of payment, credit rating and more. Influential Social Banking Index In the past two years, the Banking Supervision Department has promoted the Impact Banking Index, with the aim of creating significant social value in the activities of the supervised entities: banks and credit card companies. The influential banking project deals with the social aspects of the banking system's corporate responsibility (ESG) activity, and is aimed at strengthening the functioning and long-term impact of its activity on the socioeconomic fabric, with the understanding that the financial system plays a significant role in developing the personal, family, and business unit, by helping to realize the economic potential and can serve as a bridge to promote the periphery, financial inclusion, and promote social resilience. As it serves the majority of citizens in the country, one of the largest employers in the economy, with resources and extensive procurement activity, the banking system has the power to create change (internal and external). Influential banking challenges traditional banking to integrate environmental and social criteria as a central goal in day-to-day operations. The process of formulating the index includes a review of the leading activities in the world, as well as learning sessions with various entities from academia, social organizations, government ministries, and international bodies, in order to understand the required change and to precise the choice of topics expected to bring about change and the impact indices. After a thorough examination, 6 topics were selected to focus on: social impact management in the board of directors and management; social mobility; diversity, inclusion and equal opportunity; making services accessible for the benefit of diverse populations; dialogue with the community; Contribution and social involvement. In each of these six issues, the goal is to examine and encourage influential social behavior that goes beyond compliance with the provisions of the law. The outcome of the project is expected to be a comparative index, in the public hope, on the subject of influential banking, which will motivate the supervised entities to act, and clarify the expectations of the Supervision Department in the social sphere, while creating a strategic connection between the business model and the social challenge, in the belief that a strategic connection will create a positive and sustainable impact and encourage action and discourse regarding social responsibility. The success of the project depends greatly on the banking system's willingness to create significant social value in its activities, social value that is not produced for advertising or green washing purposes, and the degree of interest that the index will create and its influence on the public's decisions in choosing the financial institution it chooses. Since the banking system sometimes serves as a benchmark and leader in the Israeli economy, the success of the activity will be sufficient for additional organizations to adopt the index or create similar actions and expand the circles of influence. In conclusion, I would like to point out that we are all part of a whole system here. Not everything is in our hands, but we must act and sow the seeds now, each in his own plot of God, for the next generation. As I approach my expected retirement, I want to believe that I have done everything in my power to move the indicator slightly and chart the way towards improving our lives in a better society. I would like to thank the many partners, including the Rothschild Foundation, for the support and guidance of the impact supervisory teams, and for the distinguished stage, and wish you all a fruitful and enjoyable evening.

Title: Remarks by Supervisor of Banks Yair Avidan at a conference marking one year since the Open Banking Reform
text: Bank Israel Spokesperson and Economic Advocacy Bank Israel logo Jerusalem, 18 Sivan, 2023 June 07, 2023 Conference marking the one-year anniversary of the Open Banking Reform Good morning everyone, It is a great privilege and honor to open this important conference marking one year since the Open Banking reform. In fact, for the Banking Supervision Department and the banking system, the open banking project began much earlier. It is no coincidence that the law enacted at the end of 2021 went into effect within six months. You have to say things as they are. Had the Bank of Israel and the Banking Supervision Department not begun the process of formulating and shaping the reform five years earlier, we would not be standing here today when sharing information based on a uniform and international standard is already a fait accompli and is being implemented in practice. In my assessment, in our early preparations, we made it possible to implement the reform here and now, years before it would have been implemented had the whole process begun in November 2021. Already in 2016, we began regulatory steps in order to establish information sharing in the banking system, first as an enabling regulator and later as a binding. Not only did we oblige the banks to implement open banking, but later we also actively worked to select an accepted international standard, adapt it to the domestic market, and oblige the entire banking system to act according to this standard. As noted, we acted even before the legislative processes matured, with activity that entailed great risk and complexity along the way, in order to implement the standard for the Israeli market, while pushing the banking system to prepare for "this bang" as I define open banking. From the date of Bank of Israel's announcement of the adoption of the Berlin Group standard, the banking system began to act to implement it in accordance with the provisions of Proper Conduct of Banking Directive No. 368 on the subject of "Implementation of the Open Banking Standard in Israel". The first launch of the first basket of information, information about current account balances and transactions, was in April 2021. There were certainly complicated days on the eve of going on the air. Days consist mainly as a derivative of the absence of legislation. Parallel management, combined with high uncertainty, can sometimes impair the joy of doing, but moves outside the box can lead to the achievement of goals. Since then, two other significant baskets of information have gone live. In March 2022 Join information about debit card transactions and balances and in October 2022 also the information about credit and deposits became accessible and available. From the perspective of over two years, I can say that we acted wisely and am glad that we started early and implemented the implementation in stages. We expected in advance that the process of going live with the first basket would be a kind of pilot that would help examine and see the "flow of water in the pipes". As we expected, there were, and to some extent still are, certain birth pains. Some of these difficulties are completely natural, and some of them could certainly have been prevented through better Li Wei processes, development and control. It should be noted that we have also seen this phenomenon in other countries that have implemented open banking, as well as in significant projects involving many factors and diverse and complex systems. Bank Israel is committed to promoting competition and innovation in the banking system and improving the status and place of the customer. The place of the customer, but it is clear  is in the center. For this reason, the Open Banking project has been a flagship project of Bank of Israel in recent years. No other superlative can be used. Really a flagship project. The Financial Information Service Law, or by its name known as the "Open Banking Law", was enacted within the framework of the Arrangements Law and was published in November 2021, exactly three years after Bank of Israel declared the chosen standard as the "Berlin standard" for mandatory adoption in Israel. This is a very important law that will contribute greatly to strengthening the consumer and transferring power to him, to competition in the financial system, to transparency about the customer's information assets, as well as the potential for increasing financial inclusion and creating great value for the public. This is another layer in the changes in the banking and financial worlds that can move the direction and move from a slow and steady path of evolution, in which the system advances heel to thumb in a measured and orderly manner, to a path of revolution, which changes dynamically and at a rapid pace. The transition from an evolutionary process to a evolutionary process, both in terms of pace and in terms of products and services, constitutes significant potential for the development of competition and consumer welfare. At the same time, the process requires all players in the system, whether regulators, legislators, information consumers and information sources, to contribute and contribute to the proper and appropriate development of this complex system. Although at this time, it is still unclear what equilibrium the ecosystem will converge into, it is absolutely clear that without the welcome activity of all the players we will not reach a good, developing and sustainable equilibrium. We are in a significant period in which the ecosystem has opened up outside the borders of the banking system and additional entities have been given the opportunity to access information about customers. This opening greatly increases the interface between the various players in the ecosystem and the public. From the latest data, we see that there is an exponential increase in the number of requests for information (API inquiries). Last March, there were more than 28 million inquiries and there are more than 34,000 ongoing agreements to provide information. Later in the conference you will see the full data. These are nice figures, but only as opening figures. Already, 22 entities, banks, credit card companies and fintech companies operate as providers of knowledge services. I hope that soon the number of entities providing information services will increase and these entities will offer information, services, offers and great value to customers who choose to make use of it. You have to say with integrity. It's a big system, a huge amount of data, complex business processes, and a multitude of players and factors that affect it. Handling malfunctions can certainly be complex. Although we all want to be at the point in time when everything works perfectly and information flows smoothly between the different bodies, patience is required. Patience is required because the adaptation to the legislative processes and the timetable have led to relatively rapid development, and therefore there may still be problems characterized as problems of the beginning. These problems help us discover malfunctions and failures, and pushes us to constantly improve in order to minimize malfunctions and their treatment time. In light of the importance we see in the reliability and availability of information, at the end of this month an additional obligation will be introduced on sources of information relating to the SLA that they must provide within the framework of open banking, both in relation to availability and in relation to responding to inquiries received on the subject. In Europe there was one beat, and after going on the air, all the efforts were invested in stabilizing the systems. In Israel, after each phase, banking sources of information are required to add more information to open banking and prepare for the next phase, in parallel with stabilizing and correcting problems that arose in the previous phase. From here also comes the importance of working according to the uniform standard adopted in Israel. Proper use of this unified language creates the clarity and connectivity required for the proper implementation of this reform. The standard is what will also ensure the ease of connection and interfaces of information service providers to the API. This is precisely why we supported the postponement of the date of the securities information basket. The timetable set out in the legislation was in any case challenging and complex to implement. Recall that since June 2022, the banking system has been required to come up with three different versions, relating to different and complex content worlds, one of which, information on credit and deposits, implemented the Berlin Standard for the first time in the world. In particular, in January 2023, the sources of information came up with a version presenting data on small corporations and only then became available to handle the basket of information about securities. In addition, the standard of the Berlin Group's securities information basket was first published only in November 2022, and changes were required in the securities sector in order to adapt the standard to the Israeli market. Thus, only at the end of January 2023 did Bank Israel publish the binding standard in this area, and in the field of securities, we are expected to be the first in the world to implement the standard. According to accepted practice, new service providers, certainly in a complex and complicated field such as securities, require about a year of development. The shorter the development and implementation times of the standard, the greater the risk of failures in implementation and implementation. And this is a point that I would like to clarify. Quality implementation and in accordance with standards is the key to the development of open banking. In long-term terms, a delay of several months does not mean much. But rapid and low-quality development can affect and damage the public's trust in the data and the system as a whole for many years. It's a shame we'll end up in such a situation. And we should not be confused. We must be extra careful. We're dealing with information here. More specifically, sharing customer information. Information security, privacy and trust are the cornerstone of the entire ecosystem. In the absence of these, there can be no success and successful implementation of the reform. All partners have an obligation to properly manage the risks involved in information sharing, particularly information security and cyber risks. In these matters, the role of the banking system is of crucial importance. The banking system has experience and is intimately familiar with the challenges involved in managing these risks. In order to create this trust, we must all act in accordance with the rules and ensure that all processes are carried out fairly and in accordance with the law and regulation. This is from the stage of obtaining the customer's consent, through obtaining and storing the information, to making the information accessible and creating value for the customer. All of these need To be done properly and to the highest standards. This is also the reason for the heavy responsibility given to us, the various regulators, to supervise the activities of the various skyscrapers. Among other things, we are obligated to ensure that no systemic risk derived from open banking activity is created. The connectivity and the flow of data create concern about the potential for contagion and, as I noted, fear of damage to customers' trust in the banking system. We believe that the information collected about the customer's activity belongs to him and as such, the customer decides who can use the information and for what purpose. This is the "de facto" of the customer's perception at the center in this context. On the basis of this concept, the entire open banking reform is based. But we must not be satisfied with this. We must start, as we have done, with banking information, continue with information from all financial institutions, and aim to share all information about customer activity. In the current world, information is power. And just as business entities make use of the information immediately for the development and adaptation of products and services, so too will the customer be able to use the information for his personal benefit and increase his well-being. How information is used is a challenge in itself. It is too early to predict all the uses that will develop as a result of the reform, but it can certainly be said that these will support the existing trend, which is increasing. Meg What It is characterized by the strengthening of customer power, the opening of the market to competition, the unloading of products and services, the monetization of information and the entry of technology players and companies into the evolutionary financial world. All these will require a legal infrastructure and interpretation that supports and enables the development of this world. It is also certainly a significant challenge to the regulatory environment that is supposed to regulate and monitor this activity. Stable and active open banking can bring value to the customer as well as to the active players in the field. That is why we are excited and happy about the opening of the ecosystem beyond the borders of the banking system and the entry of new players who will use this amazing infrastructure to benefit consumers. This is certainly the beginning, but certainly not the end of the road. This is only a stage on the way of market development to finding the right equilibrium point, although it is possible that it will be dynamic and change with the development of the system, the composition of the players, collaborations and more. We are pleased that there is room to promote an open financial system in which the client, according to his choice, will choose the manner in which he will consume his services, as well as allow the use of the information asset he owns. In this way, customers will be able to receive value propositions and more tailored products, better advice, more diverse service, a better customer experience, and financial inclusion in a variety of financial services and products. The value overflow is what will justify the enormous costs involved in implementing the open banking reform, and it will be the basis of the business model of the various information service providers. The banking system is a very significant source of data. Alongside the risks of implementing the reform, there are also opportunities. We are witnessing new and advanced models for activity around the world, including embedded banking, banking as a service platform, and banking as an aggregator of information and other models. There is a "blue ocean" here, and it is right that we act in it correctly without harming the environment. Collaborations and cooperation between parts of the system will help lay the right infrastructure on which we will build the next floor. This reform is the first step and the cornerstone for realizing the vision and strategy of establishing and creating an open financial world, a world in which not only banks serve as sources of information, but it is a world in which data on long-term savings and the pension world are also integrated, and later on, we must act to a world of "open economy", a stage in which we will realize the vision "Open Data"  the open data stage, an activity whose buds can already be detected around the world. Open banking is expected to develop not only in the field of information but also in the field of payments, and we continue to learn from what is happening in the world. It is also an excellent opportunity to pay tribute and thank everyone who took part in this important project. To employees of the Bank of Israel and the Banking Supervision Department, members of the Securities Authority and the Ministry of Finance who contributed, each in his field, to the realization of the vision. To the various entities that serve as sources of information, at this time, banks and credit card companies whose information constitutes a cornerstone for the existence of the open world. And, of course, to information service providers whose work will maximize the value of open banking and help externalize and leverage information in a better and more accurate way for customers. All of these and many others play an important part in building the new world we are at our doorstep, and I think we can all be proud of our work and its expected impact on the public and the economy. I would like to thank everyone for their cooperation and determination and for the great privilege I had to take part in the implementation of this significant reform. Thank you very much and continue a fruitful conference.

Title: Remarks by outgoing Supervisor of Banks Yair Avidan at a farewell event
text: Remarks by outgoing Supervisor of Banks Yair Avidan at a farewell event "So here they are, three full years have passed since I took office. Three years of intensity, totality and exhaustion. As far as I'm concerned, extraction is satisfactory and meaningful. In a world of mission and contribution to the economy and society, it is difficult to think of a role and mission with a much higher fulfillment." 12/06/2023 To view the speech as a file click here My dear family, the Governor of the Bank of Israel and the honorable all, It is certainly challenging to find a language that connects the broad common denominator of the participants in this event. Apologies in advance for the burden and to some extent for the insufficient curse. In recent years, the Israeli banking system has demonstrated impressive stability, supported economic growth, assisted in the activity of the Israeli economy, and fulfilled its role in the socioeconomic fabric of the country. The stability of the domestic banking system, which is taken for granted by many, is reinforced by recent events in the global financial system. This stability was achieved thanks to the activity of the Bank of Israel and the Banking Supervision Department, which maintains close supervision and control through a variety of powers and tools designed to ensure the proper functioning of the banking corporations. At the same time, the Banking Supervision Department has acted extensively, and even more intensively in recent years, to promote fairness in the relationship between banking corporations and their customers. Customer trust in the Israeli banking system is the cornerstone of the entire system, and a culture that advocates fair relations and quality service plays a large part in creating and maintaining this trust. The social expectation from the banks is intensifying and expanding to issues that receive central status and paramount importance, including the demand for extensive involvement and social responsibility, strengthening and maintaining the values of equality, financial inclusion of all populations, and thinking and dealing with weighty issues regarding the future of society and the future of the planet in which we live. The banking industry has undergone a revolution in recent years and is much more competitive today than in the past. Financial products and services are unloaded and offered by other players and through various technological platforms. Financial information about customers, which in the past was the domain of the banking corporations only, is now available in an open and accessible manner and enables the provision of services and value propositions tailored to the customer's character and the characteristics of his activity. The Banking Supervision Department has worked extensively to remove barriers, increase transparency, and promote competition in order to transfer power to the customer and strengthen his competitive power. This trend of increased competition is expected to continue in the coming years with the completion and maturation of many measures initiated and promoted by the Banking Supervision Department. Looking ahead, 2023 is accompanied by a sharp increase in uncertainty. In the domestic arena, the increase in uncertainty stems from the potential for advancing significant legislative changes relating to the Israeli legal system without broad consensus, which, insofar as they harm the independence and strength of institutions, are liable to harm the stability and prosperity of the Israeli economy over time, and are also reflected in the results of the banking system. And now, three full years have passed since I took office. I took office at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic - a point in time of a world in turmoil, an economy and a world of banking and finance in a state of uncertainty, with all the effects on the public. The end point also seems to be challenging in these aspects and the characteristics are similar, although, the circumstances are different. There were no days of grace. Not even minutes. Empty offices. Meetings by phone and, at best, by Tims or Zoom. Life in 2D. My first day in office was the day the Israeli economy emerged from the first wave of the coronavirus. We had no idea whether this was the last wave and/or how many waves remained. The uncertainty was great. As part of this COVID- 19 pandemic, we acted and greatly assisted the banking system and the Israeli economy in overcoming the many difficulties that accompanied this global pandemic. And it is hard to say that the past three years have been typical years in the life of the state, economy, society, the world of banking and supervision, and to a certain extent, also at the global level and the global economy. Suffice it to say from above the following:  Five waves of coronavirus  Instability in the political situation in Israel (three elections)  The inflation and interest rate environment  War of Russia Ukraine  Challenges of business continuity and functional continuity (Corona; Guardian of the Walls; Dawn; Shield and Arrow)  A global banking environment in which we have seen institutions whose stability is undermined  Challenges to the business model and profitability of the banking system  Managing the tension between stability, encouraging competition and consumer welfare  Uncertainty in aspects of the structure of financial supervision and more Amidst the complexity of the beginning of the term and the uncertainty as a supervisor, we defined several main objectives in light of which we operated:  Maintaining stability and safeguarding depositors' money  Instilling a culture that is fair, inclusive and impactful to customers  Establishing a competitive and advanced financial system for the benefit of customers  and adapting the Banking Supervision Department's activity to the changing financial and technological environment Over the past three years, we have worked to implement and realize our goals through a large number of steps and activities, including: accompanying the establishment of a new digital bank and granting a license to another digital bank; Accompanying the establishment of a computer services bureau that reduces barriers to entry into the banking industry; completing and operating a one-click bank account mobility system that enables easy passage for customers who choose to switch banks and strengthens the competitive power of banking system customers; removing barriers to the use of cloud systems that will enable the banking system to operate efficiently, flexibly, and innovatively; Implementation of the open banking reform that enables sharing of information with other parties and leveraging information belonging to and for the benefit of the customer; promoting innovation, unloading services and financial products; publication for the first time of average interest rates at the bank level, in order to strengthen comparative capabilities and bargaining power; a mortgage reform that simplifies the product and enables transparency for customers and better comparison options; promoting the banking system's preparedness to deal with climate and environmental risks; and continuing to strengthen and improve cyber defense and the envelope that supports this activity. Significant emphasis is placed on improving fairness in relations between banks and customers, with customer perception at the center leading the way, inter alia, through directives defining the banks' conduct when providing service, increasing control and consumer enforcement activity, including imposing sanctions on the system, freezing current account fees, formulating a methodology for measuring fairness, and a variety of additional measures designed to implement a fair, inclusive and influential culture. In this we will only mention the promotion of the Financial Availability Charter for dealing with economic violence, the promotion of a charter to make banking services accessible to senior citizens, activity to increase financial awareness in Arab society, and the promotion of influential banking in the banking system. Alongside all this, of course, we invested heavily in ensuring and establishing the stability of the banking system, we acted to monitor, supervise and control, we ensured that relevant and current regulation was maintained, and of course, we operated within the frameworks and tools at our disposal in auditing, evaluation, lines of activity, enforcement, and more. And I will sin against the truth if I do not mention even in a nutshell activities in the fields of information and knowledge, managing model risks on the challenges inherent in the subject, promoting and enabling the complex worlds of AH and terrorism, strengthening and leveraging international ties (UAE, Bahrain, US regulators and central bodies - IMF, OECD, trade agreements, prospectuses, rating companies) and more. Indeed, a very wide range of topics, fields and activities. And from what we have done, there is room to look at the present and the expected developments, as much as it is possible to predict and evaluate them. The conservatism inherent in the traditional banking world is fertile ground for significant disruption and disruption processes. These processes have led to the fact that at this time it can be clearly said that the banking market is no longer on the slow and steady path of evolution, in which the system is advancing heel to thumb in a measured and orderly manner, but is on the unstable path of evolution, which is changing dynamically and at a rapid pace. The evolutionary process is already changing today and is expected to continue to change, within a relatively short time, conventions, processes, methods and cultures that we have known, and to create a different world. In my opinion, the new situation that will stabilize when it stabilizes and as it stabilizes, can be called the New Normal, and it will be different from the one we know today. The challenge of seeing the customer at the center has become complex in light of the increase in life expectancy, various social and ethnic aspects, alongside an ever-expanding range of services and products. Empowering the digital services provided by the banking system to its customers has contributed greatly to the increase in consumer welfare and service experience. Digital activity and operational efficiency create an inherent tension vis-a-vis the deployment and availability of traditional branches and services, which is expressed mainly among various disadvantaged populations. This requires all of us to be attentive, sensitive and sometimes even compassionate. The subject corresponds with the role and challenges of the banking system in the socioeconomic fabric and its importance of being influential. The impact must be from the perception of values and the assimilation of such a culture. This concept has something much broader in it than marginal activity or momentary profitability. It has a kind of vision, a long-term concept that requires investment and one that creates a deep and real impact on the communities in which we operate. Such a concept can differentiate the banking system from the evolving competitive environment, and take advantage of the disruption to strengthen and leverage the relationship with customers and society as a whole while increasing loyalty and trust. The social expectation from the banks is intensifying and expanding to issues that receive central status and paramount importance, including the demand for extensive involvement and social responsibility, strengthening and maintaining the values of equality, financial inclusion of all populations, and thinking and dealing with weighty issues regarding the future of society. While the banking system should not be leading some of these activities, it must not be left behind, and we have an obligation to direct, support, and assist in dealing with these issues. And I will try from a place of humility and humility, to outline some of the forward-looking challenges, of course, that take on a different dimension and depth in different time frames. In the consumer-competitive world, it is important to continue empowering and strengthening the customer's vision at the center. There is no doubt that as a society we face a significant challenge when it comes to financial literacy, digital literacy and information literacy. A broad and comprehensive public response is required that will enable our parents, us, children and grandchildren to be more intelligent and involved consumers, alongside making banking services accessible through the various service channels. It is true that this will be expressed by deepening and expanding the transparency of information to the customer regarding products, services, commissions and conditions in an accessible and simple manner, improving financial literacy to empower customers and strengthening their ability to make informed decisions, fostering customer experiences and journeys that will improve consumer loyalty and competitiveness, with an emphasis on personalized services, effective mechanisms for resolving complaints and convenient access channels according to the customer's characteristics and needs. All this alongside compliance and observance of privacy and consumer protection laws. We all have the task of developing and strengthening the public's sense of responsibility for its financial situation and encouraging it to show initiative and involvement. The Banking Supervision Department has advanced many reforms in recent years, the main purpose of which is to strengthen the customer's power and increase his bargaining power through the information and new tools created by these reforms. In order to derive significant value from these reforms, customers must know and make use of them and exercise their increased competitive power through engagement, initiative and intelligent consumerism. It is our duty to continue to promote the necessary measures in order to strengthen the customer on the one hand, and to carry out effective information and mediation to the clients on the other, so that they can derive the maximum benefit. And in terms of customer service, we need to continue to intensify the way customer complaints are handled. It is of utmost importance to focus on maintaining and continually strengthening an efficient and fair complaint handling process that advocates, inter alia, timely resolution of customer complaints, improving communication with customers and means of learning from customer feedback to improve products and services. And with the increasing use of customer data, it is important and necessary to strengthen security measures and data privacy protections. Challenge and importance in implementing strong cybersecurity protocols, complying with data protection regulations and ensuring responsible handling of customer information. In this context, it is necessary to note information processing tools, the development of advanced technology-based capabilities, such as artificial intelligence (Al), machine learning (ML) and communication between computers (API). These technologies are expected to transform from a supportive means to a central and dominant factor in decision-making processes in various content worlds, including the financial world. The benefits of using information and advanced models are clear and undeniable. However, this activity is not without difficulties and risks, and therefore the technology must be implemented and used carefully and responsibly. One of the significant risks is related to ethical issues of discrimination, and various biases that may arise in models. These may be expressed in prohibited discrimination against customers. Alongside this, there are additional risks such as incorrect planning of business decision-making mechanisms, the creation of a "black box" and loss of transparency, harm to privacy protection and other issues. In the prudential world, but not only, governance and the culture of organizational risk management must continue to be strengthened. Professional, effective and efficient risk management is essential for maintaining stability, as well as emphasizing traditional, current and evolving risk management. And by the way of innovation and digital transformation, the adoption of technological progress is essential for the existence and development of a competitive and even existential environment. The system must invest in digital infrastructure, continue to innovate, even more vigorously, legacy systems, and provide user-friendly and convenient digital platforms, while providing a safe environment. And within the framework of innovation and technology, in order to take an active part in the development of the ecosystem, there is certainly room to promote collaborations with fintech companies, start- ups and other financial institutions that can bring disruptive innovations and create new opportunities for growth. Within this framework, it is important to plan strategically, to continuously assess and analyze the development of the competitive environment, market trends and emerging technologies, understanding changing customer expectations, anticipating competitive threats, and adjusting business models accordingly. And a few words about climate and environmental risks. Climate change presents us with special challenges that we reach without previous experience. This is true both of the necessity of reducing the pace of climate change, and of the need to prepare for what seems difficult to prevent. These two courses of action are a national mission of the highest order. I am convinced that through cooperation between all the relevant players - the government, regulators, the business sector and the general public - much can and should be done to advance on these two paths. Central banks and supervisors responsible for financial stability also have a significant role to play in this matter, but it is important to understand that the activity of financial regulators is complementary and cannot replace the activity required of governments. In this spirit, and against the background of the emerging climate crisis, more and more governments and business entities - financial and real - are committing to ESG goals, particularly climate goals, and striving for a better world. In other words, more and more key players in human society are realizing that "we must reset!" First, to "reset ourselves" so that we understand the magnitude of the event and react accordingly, as well as reset in the crucial sense at hand - zero greenhouse gas emissions and achieving the Net-Zero goal. We, as the regulator of the banking system, and the banks are partners in this change in thinking. According to the 2023 report recently released by the World Economic Forum (WEF), environmental and climate risks have once again been ranked as the No. 1 threat threatening us over the next decade. These are also the risks we are least prepared for. In the global and local response to climate change, we must take a determined approach and a long-term view. Passivity on the subject is not a relevant alternative. The cost of "not acting" may be higher than the cost of "acting." The banking system can help meet these targets. The Banking Supervision Department at Bank Israel is acting and will continue to act in order to be in Best Practice in accompanying and managing this activity. And of course, without additional social emphasis, the puzzle will be missing. Harvard University has developed the concept of "shared value" over the past decade. Behind this concept is the notion that to remain competitive in today's world, companies need to do more than just monetize. They need to create shared value, that is, to create economic value in a way that also addresses social or environmental needs, bringing about a profound change in strategic thinking and business model. Through this conceptual shift, businesses differentiate themselves, open new paths of growth for themselves, and also achieve better bottom lines. From a business perspective, creating "shared value" is a way to gain a significant competitive advantage. At the same time, a shared value can "make the pie bigger", which is an important value in itself. And in my view, not all financial profits are equal. Profits generated while providing social value have a higher strategic value. Companies should act out of a mission and purpose and not just in order to maximize financial profits. Businesses, and in this the banking system, it is right, and even an obligation, that they take responsibility and positively influence their human and physical environment - in my view, this is part of the "license to operate". And I assume that all of us here understand that a strong company needs a strong regulator, and we in the Banking Supervision Department are acting and will act to continue to be strong enough. We work to realize our vision of being leaders, initiators and professionals for the benefit of the economy and society. The challenge becomes only complex and challenging, whether we are dealing with the multiplicity of planes or the rate of change or the size and scope of the field of action. There is a significant challenge of preserving and strengthening human capital. Used and developed technological means to support activity. Challenge in responding to the development of business models. Challenge in understanding and assessing emerging and evolving risks. A challenge in understanding what is permitted and what is prohibited in light of the existing legal and regulatory infrastructure. The entry of new players. The challenge of sharing and coordinating with regulators and many stakeholders and partners. The challenge is enormous. The range is wide. Responsibility is high. So here they are, three full years have passed since I took office. Three years of intensity, totality and exhaustion. As far as I'm concerned, extraction is satisfactory and meaningful. In a world of mission and contribution to the economy and society, it is difficult to think of a role and mission with much higher utilization. But it is impossible to conclude without a few more words of thanks and appreciation. I would like to thank the Governor for his trust and support all along. I would like to thank my colleagues in the management of Bank Israel for their partnership. I would like to thank all stakeholders and partners, regulators, representatives of the various ministries (finance, justice, environmental protection, social equality, economy, construction and housing) for their cooperation. I would like to thank all supervisors for maintaining professional, challenging, contributing, respectful and respectful supervisor-supervisor relations. And when you are looked at by the supervisory staff, it is hard not to be amazed by your activity, the sense of mission and dedication of so many employees. I met and had the privilege, the duty and the challenge to be with serious, professional and dedicated people who care for all citizens of the country. I am grateful for the great privilege given to me to lead the Banking Supervision Department in recent years. And there is no better opportunity to wish success to the incoming supervisor, Dani Khakhiashvili. An excellent appointment that I am convinced will continue to lead the Supervision Department to impressive achievements. Good luck Danny. Now I want to be a son, spouse, father, grandfather and of course I will look for and consider the challenges and paths suitable for the future, places where I can contribute and benefit so that we will live here in a better, fairer and more equal society. Thank you.

Title: Israel's policy of integration in the global economy: the difficulties
Subtitle: Speech by Mr David Klein, Governor of the Bank of Israel, to The Directors' Forum, The Association of Electronics and Information Industries, Tel Aviv, 29 April 2001
text: David Klein: Israels policy of integration in the global economy: the difficulties Speech by Mr David Klein, Governor of the Bank of Israel, to The Directors Forum, The Association of Electronics and Information Industries, Tel Aviv, 29 April 2001. * * * 1. The economic strategy For the past decade the object of Israels macroeconomic policy has been to achieve economic integration within the global economy. The main aspects of this policy are well known:  Reducing tariffs and abolishing non-tariff barriers, so that goods and services can move freely;  Removing foreign-currency control, enabling the free flow of capital;  Introducing structural changes to render the economy more competitive and reduce the governments share in it;  Adopting international standards of economic management, inter alia in the macroeconomic sphere, the most prominent among them being to adhere to the fiscal discipline required in order to reduce the governments debt burden, and to attain price stability via an independent central bank. The logic underlying this policy is two-fold:  Contending with competition in world markets will require us to become more specialized and more efficient. Utilizing the resources available to us, this will result in a higher growth rate.  Abolishing foreign-currency control, introducing structural changes, and adopting international standards of economic management will enable us to build another stratum on this basis: improving the investment climate and attracting foreign capital to Israel. As a result, Israel will be able to finance investment not only by domestic saving but also by foreign saving, making an even faster growth rate possible. We are evidently referring to a policy that focuses on sustainable growth accompanied by an ongoing increase in productivity, and led by a rise in investments and exports; while the improvement of the standard of living is not the leading factor, but the result of that structure, alongside adherence to budgetary restraint and price stability. This policy differs substantially from that adopted in the first four decades of Israels existence, although it embodies elements-such as tariff-reduction-that have been on the agenda in the past. On the other hand, the change in Israel was made possible because of the significant shift towards globalization in the world at large. Nonetheless, the adoption of the new approach, in all its aspects, has not gone smoothly. Many interests and habits were based on the old framework, and although the number of advocates of the old view is dwindling they are still able to drag out the process of change unduly, as they did in the last decade. My aim here is to describe some of the difficulties that confronted us in the last decade in attempting to implement the new approach. 2. The difficulties in adapting the policy instruments a. The first difficulty: the exchange-rate regime This difficulty kept cropping up, for two reasons:  Foreign-currency liberalization cannot exist alongside a fixed exchange rate such as existed in Israel, between depreciations, for about 40 years. The combination of the free flow of capital and a government commitment to a given exchange rate is a prescription for speculation and financial crises. 34/2001 1  On the other hand, Israels exchange rate, especially since the Economic Stabilization Program of 1985, served as a nominal anchor, i.e., the main instrument for stabilizing inflation at a low level was supposed to be a fixed exchange rate. This contradiction between the need to make the exchange-rate regime more flexible because of the liberalization and the need to fix it in order to stabilize inflation had to be resolved. It is worth noting here that in every transition process, whenever we encountered basic dilemmas that obliged us to decide which path to take, we always asked ourselves what other countries did in similar circumstances. In general, we aspired to re-invent as few wheels as possible, saving our creativity  such as it was  for other matters. Thus, using the experience of others, we adopted the following solution:  The exchange rate would be gradually made more flexible, parallel to the liberalization process. This began early in 1989, when the exchange rate band was first introduced, and continued when its determination was transferred to the market five years later, in 1994;  Its place as a nominal anchor would be taken by the short-term interest rate, to be determined by the Bank of Israel in view of the inflation target; this transition was also implemented gradually.  That shift turned out to be difficult for various elements:  Those, mainly in the business community, who had become accustomed to a policy of a fixed exchange rate (thus, for example, the transition from a horizontal to a crawling band at the end of 1991 was still being justified by the need to give economic agents engaged in international trade greater long-term certainty regarding the development of the exchange rate-a commitment that could not be met, as has been proved innumerable times in the history of exchange-rate bands).  Those in the policy-making community who still believed in the exchange rate as a nominal anchor: they continued to vigorously oppose each stage of the relaxation of exchange-rate controls. These elements continue to this day to resist the abolition of the exchange-rate band, even though their reasons have changed and it is perfectly clear that it will be impossible to defend it should the need arise.  Those who did not like the by-product of the change under which the Bank of Israel acquired greater independence in managing monetary policy: the tradition in Israel is that changes in the exchange rate can be made only with the agreement of the Ministry of Finance, while changes in the interest rate can be made solely on the basis of the Bank of Israels decision. The person who immediately grasped that aspect of the change-although that was not the reason it was introduced-was the Minister of Finance, Yitzhak Modai, when the shift was made from a horizontal to a crawling exchange-rate band, in December 1991.  One question still remains open: can the Bank of Israels intervention in the foreign-currency market serve, in certain circumstances, objectives that are also important for the central bank? This question can be placed on the agenda once the exchange-rate band has been abolished. In the last three years the Bank of Israel has refrained from intervening in the foreign-currency market in any way. As long as that policy continues, changes in the Bank of Israels foreign-exchange reserves can result primarily from the governments foreign-currency cash flow, because only the government has direct access to the Bank of Israel for selling and buying foreign currency, and from profits made from investing the reserves. There are small changes from time to time because of shifts in the banks voluntary deposits with the Bank of Israel. The level of the reserves is not affected, as some still think, by private capital flows and interest-rate differentials. Only a few days ago an analyst explained in an interview why Israels foreign-currency market is not a classic target for assault by foreign speculators. One of the reasons for this, he claimed, was that the foreign-currency reserves are very high (Maariv, 17.4.2001). Since we are not active in the market, there is no relevance in this context to the question of how large our foreign-currency reserves are. 2 34/2001 b. The second difficulty: managing monetary policy so as to attain price stability in a regime of inflation targets Israels economic integration within the global economy requires inter alia accepting the standard of price stability prevailing in the developed countries, obtained via an independent central bank. This transition also created several difficulties:  At one time the slogan inflation isnt everything, meaning that other objectives such as growth and employment also need to be considered, was very popular. The debate was conducted between those who believed that expansionary monetary policy (i.e., reducing the interest rate) could stimulate employment and those who thought that the end-result would only be inflation which, if it persisted, would eventually increase unemployment. The discussion of this subject was concluded in the world, and the general consensus comes down to the following two points:  Monetary policy has to be geared first of all towards maintaining price stability;  To the extent that it does not contradict that primary aim, interest-rate policy can also be administered so as to aid the government in attaining other policy objectives.  As long as we were endeavoring to reduce the inflation rate-until two years ago-the argument as to whether price stability was at all possible in Israel continued. It was claimed that it was not feasible because of structural reasons, defined as nominal rigidities or a monopolistic structure. In any case, a low inflation rate was said to be achievable in Israel only if it was latent, in which case it would be bound to re-emerge at the first opportunity. For example, a low inflation rate would be possible only with a large balance-of-payments deficit and cheap imports flooding the economy-an unsustainable situation. Thus, according to this scenario, there would eventually be massive devaluation, followed by accelerated inflation. The inevitable conclusion was that it would be better not to try to eliminate inflation, as it would not last. We appear by now to have acquired sufficient experience to be able to see that this argument was baseless. On the basis of these considerations, until 2000 the government continued to display reluctance to set annual inflation targets (it deferred determining a target for as long as possible, leaving it to the end of the year, ignoring the logic regarding the lags with which monetary policy takes effect; from time to time it considered accepting the inevitability of rising inflation; it refused to set a long-term or final target). In August 2000 conditions were created in which the government decided to adopt a target of price stability for 2003 and subsequently. This brought to an end a period in which it was necessary each year to take a stand with regard to the inflation target. The target from now on is to maintain price stability, defined as an annual inflation rate in the range of 1 percent to 3 percent.  In the Bank of Israel, too, the shift to managing a policy based on inflation targets created difficulties. In the first half of the 1990s we were still wavering between reducing unemployment and lowering the inflation rate; between defending the exchange rate so that it did not deviate far from the mid-point of the band and aiming for price stability. In 1994 the inflation rate was 14.5 percent, compared with a target of 8 percent-the most outstanding failure of monetary policy in the last decade-and in mid-1996 inflation expectations were still 14 percent. Altogether, 199596 was a period of impending crisis. Fiscal policy was at breaking-point because of growing deficits, and monetary policy was contending with a new problem: defending the lower limit of the exchange-rate band against the massive capital inflow of billions of dollars while persevering with the effort to attain the inflation target. Only in the last third of the 1990s did inflation start declining, albeit not continuously, towards price stability. The lack of focus in the first half of the decade obliged us to display greater decisiveness in conducting monetary policy in the second half, so that we could indeed advance towards the target.  The list of difficulties would be incomplete without mentioning the need to uproot all the habits and institutionalized arrangements acquired and established in the long years of inflation in order to enable us to live in peace with it. Most prominent among them are the arrangements with regard to public-sector wages, the various kinds of indexation in the goods and services markets, and inflation-adjusted taxation and reporting regulations. The government needs to address all these issues in order to get rid of them once and for all. 34/2001 3 c. The third difficulty: managing fiscal policy in order to reduce government debt In this sphere, too, several problems have arisen:  First, there was a longstanding tradition in Israel and the world according to which the budget can serve as a counter-cyclical instrument, with a surplus during a period of prosperity and a deficit during a slump. Experience shows that it is easier to create a deficit in a slump than to maintain a surplus in a period of prosperity. The result is rising government debt, an increase in the share of debt-servicing costs in the budget, and a heavier tax burden. The conclusion throughout the developed world was that priority has to be given to reducing government debt to a reasonable level by limiting the budget deficit, and to easing the tax burden by cutting government expenditure as a share of GDP. This conclusion has not yet been accepted by everybody in Israel, even though the basic approach has been adopted by all governments in the last decade.  Second, the way the budget deficit was defined in Israel differed from that in the rest of the world, so that our measured deficit was significantly lower than it would have been had the generally-accepted definition been used. This misled many people, including prime ministers and members of the government, made it very difficult to compare the situation in Israel with the rest of the world, and also hampered efforts to explain the need to reduce the deficit. The advocates of our own special method of defining the deficit, which is still used, claimed that it is more correct and refused to change it. For years the Bank of Israel has avoided arguing about which definition is more correct, suggesting that both figures be presented to the government and the public, but so far without any success. The reduction of inflation has served to greatly narrow the gap between the two definitions, but has not eliminated it completely. Naturally, it is not difficult, statistically or otherwise, to measure and present the deficit in the same way as is done elsewhere, and it is time we did so.  Third, the need to adhere to fiscal discipline over the long run requires a change of approach in setting the order of priorities in allocating government resources. Whereas in the past it was possible to solve any problem, whether genuine or imaginary, by increasing expenditure and the government debt, the need to maintain the declining path of government expenditure-albeit not absolutely but as a share of GDP-raises new issues all over the world, for example:  Should the social services that the government provides be extended universally or depend on a means test? Should the governments plans to reduce poverty make a distinction between people of working age and others?  Is there a place for private services alongside the public services in the spheres of education, health, and welfare?  Should the government be the sole agent involved in developing and operating the economic infrastructure, or is there room for the activity of private for-profit elements in part of it, in accordance with a framework determined by the government? In Israel, too, we have begun dealing with these and other questions, but we are still a long way away from their implementation as an integral, routine aspect of the long-term effort that features prominently-as it rightly should-in the governments discussions of the budget. In the world in general considerable progress has been made on these subjects, extensive experience has been acquired by other governments, and we can and should benefit from it; there is no need to invent everything ourselves. 3. Coping with problems of adaptation A decade of administering a macroeconomic policy designed to open up the economy and reduce the governments share in economic activity, against the backdrop of the changing geopolitical situation, has served to create closer economic integration between Israel and the rest of the world. There no longer seems to be anyone who disagrees with the view that this is the way to fulfill Israels potential for sustainable economic growth. An organic part of this approach is to adhere to accepted standards of economic management, including fiscal discipline, price stability, and an exchange rate that is 4 34/2001 determined by market forces. This framework obliges us to cope with several additional problems, some of them as yet unresolved, as we have just seen. Because of the extensive economic involvement of foreign elements in Israel that is a result of that policy, we are subject to constant review by foreign analysts, who rank our economic performance. In addition, many of Israels foreign liabilities and assets are traded on international stock markets, which also continually indicate their confidence in us. We are not isolated from the rest of the world, and we must grow accustomed to that idea in order to continue developing the economy, creating jobs, and raising the standard of living. 34/2001 5

Title: Three differences between Israel and the US in the 'quality of the environment' in managing monetary policy
Subtitle: Address by Mr David Klein, Governor of the Bank of Israel, to the Israel-America Chamber of Commerce, held in Tel-Aviv, 10 May 2001.
text: David Klein: Three differences between Israel and the US in the 'quality of the environment in managing monetary policy Address by Mr David Klein, Governor of the Bank of Israel, to the Israel-America Chamber of Commerce, held in Tel-Aviv, 10 May 2001. * * * The background On 3 January, 2001, after the US Federal Reserve announced the first interest-rate cut of the year, the demand was made that the Bank of Israel follow suit. The demand was reiterated after the additional interest-rate reductions that followed. No such demand had been made in 1999 and 2000, when the Fed raised interest several times, so that it had to be assumed that the demand to follow suit was no more than an attempt to vary the list of reasons, which changes from time to time, behind the demand that is always on the agenda in Israel to reduce the interest rate, and the faster the better. Nevertheless, it may be instructive to consider the differences between Israel and the US in referring to the management of monetary policy. Understanding these differences can shed light on the question of whether it is reasonable to automatically imitate the Fednaturally only when it reduces interest. The differences What, then, are the differences? 1. The culture of inflation Ever since the trauma that Americans experienced in the wake of the oil crisis of the 1970s, when the inflation rate reached an intolerable level of 13.5 percent in 1980, there has been no argument in the US regarding the need to keep inflation low. The US has no formal inflation target, and the law  which has not changed in this respect in the last 50 years  instructs the central bank to relate to growth and employment, too. Despite all this, throughout the 1980s the American central bank focused on getting the annual inflation rate down, to the 2-3 percent that has characterized the last eight years. The unemployment rate ranged from 5 to 7 percent all those years, and still the central bank did not relent. The message was: employment is generated not by accepting inflation but by making structural changes and raising productivity. Thus, ultimately, the unemployment rate declined to 4 percent, and the US economy showed that maintaining price stability does in fact go hand in hand with reducing unemployment. The upshot is that the US consumer is prepared to invest time in comparing prices and to travel quite a long way to buy the same product for less money. At any rate, the Cent is still legal tender, and the efforts to replace the one-dollar note with a coin have not succeeded. As you know, the Agora is no longer legal tender in Israel, though it still features in prices, and an interesting debate is currently being held about the rules of price-rounding when payment is in cash. Anyone who thinks that the rules of price-rounding are simple  after all, this was settled in the Bank of Israel Law  should study the proposed law on the subject that has already passed its first reading in the Knesset. In addition, the note with the smallest value is the NIS 20, and it is quite a long time since the NIS 10 note was replaced by a coin. Despite the differences in average income, the attitude of the Israeli consumer to money and prices seems to be somewhat less careful than that of his American counterpart, and he is also somewhat less confident that the low inflation rate will persist. It is hardly surprising. When actual inflation deviated upwards from the target people said that this constituted a proof that it was impossible to lower the inflation rate in Israel. When the deviation was downwards, they said that the Bank of Israel had failed  as if monetary policy was an exact science and the interest rate a laser beam. When the inflation rate diverged upwards from the target, people said that the target had to be raised, and that a little more inflation was preferable to a little more unemployment; and when it diverged downwards from the target people said that a commission of inquiry should be set up and, naturally, the Governor dismissed. The Chairman of the Federal Reserve in the US once defined 'price stability' as a situation in which no-one considers inflation as something that has to be taken into account in economic decisions. Apparently we have not yet reached the 39/2001 1 stage where we regard low inflation and price stability as natural. We still require proof, and that obliges Israel's central bank to be a little less indifferent than its US counterpart to threats to price stability. Thus, anyone who claims that the Fed thinks that there is substitutability between inflation and growth, and that it now tends to prefer growth to inflation, is mistaken. The Fed is reducing the interest rate aggressively because it is indeed convinced that it is needed in order to shorten the period of slowdown in the US economy, but this policy is undertaken on the assumption that it will not accelerate inflation. This assumption is based on both the rise in productivity that characterizes the era of information technology and the longstanding credibility that the Fed has acquired in its struggle to maintain price stability. In that, too, we are very different from them. 2. The dollar and the shekel The dollar, as you know, is a currency that many people in many countries are prepared to use as a means of payment and hold in order to maintain the value of their assets. The shekel, as you know, has not yet attained that status. It is true that because of the decline in the inflation rate we have stopped running after the dollar, but the habit of linking the prices of certain goods and services to the dollar has not yet disappeared. That provides the background for the fact that the balance-of-payments deficit has been part of the American scene for many years. In the last year, for example, it amounted to 400 billion  about 4.5 percent of GDP. Till now the Americans had no real difficulty financing their import surplus. The world was willing to take the difference in dollars, which were invested in various assets in the US. Foreign investment in US Treasury bonds alone is nearly a massive 1,300 billion. Our situation is, of course, very different. Although for us, too, a balance-of-payments deficit is a matter of routine, we cannot finance it with our currency. In other words, both we and the Americans need dollars in order to cover the import surplus. The difference is that they can print them. We need to borrow them or, as has happened in recent years, benefit from the foreign investment in Israel that has enabled us to maintain an import surplus without increasing our foreign debt, and even to accrue foreign-currency reserves and reduce our past foreign debt. Naturally, all this was possible because our balance-of-payments deficit shrank significantly. This was not the case in the mid-1990s, for example, when the deficit amounted to 6 percent of GDP  a rate that was taken as signalling an approaching crisis. The fears were so great that in deciding on its economic policy targets for 1997 the government placed the need to reduce the balance-of-payments deficit first, before growth, and certainly before reducing inflation (the inflation target set for 1997 was 7-10 percent). That balance-of-payments deficit had grown because fiscal and monetary policy was loose, there had been economic growth because of the rise in consumption and the standard of living, and that had brought both the balance-of-payments deficit and inflation in its wake. Only the policy shift saved us from certain disaster, teaching us once again the lesson that we have learned several times in the past: growth led by consumption cannot be sustainable in Israel. The Americans, on the other hand, are building on that alone to revive their economy. Both their monetary and their fiscal policy are expansionary  the former by rapid interest  rate reduction and the latter by tax reduction  in order to stimulate growth through an increase in private consumption. If as a result there is a rise in the balance-of-payments deficit, so be it. It is true that from time to time somebody stands up and says that things cannot go on like that, but so far it has worked. Maybe because the alternatives are less appealing. Another angle of the same situation is that US Secretaries of the Treasury advocate a strong dollar, while Israeli Ministers of Finance prefer a weak shekel. 3. The financial markets The third difference lies in the structure of the financial markets. It is widely known that the US has the most developed financial markets in the world. In the last few years the Nasdaq has attracted widespread publicity, but the main point is that the Americans have a developed system of non-bank financial intermediation, comprising inter alia a huge market for both Treasury and corporate bonds. There are also markets for the financial instruments that have developed in the last twenty years, primarily derivatives of various kinds on interest rates, exchange rates, and share prices. In addition, there is an institutional system outside commercial banking that includes investment banks, financing 2 39/2001 institutions, asset- and financial-management services, and brokers of various kinds, offering a variety of financial services. And what about us?  The stock market may be replete with companies registered for trading, representing a large number relative to the size of our economy, but with a small turnover and a concentrated ownership structure. All this is despite the fact that the management of the stock exchange has done all it could  and even more  to introduce trading and clearing systems that are among the most advanced in the world.
